subsubtopic: PROPOSED FREE TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my honour and duty to present a petition on behalf of a number of residents of Canada who are concerned that without any mandate from the Canadian people the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has negotiated a bilateral trade deal with the U.S. In spite of his promise that sovereignty would not be compromised, the proposed trade deal threatens the fabric of Canadian political and economic sovereignty and our ability to establish economic programs to our own benefit. It also fails to secure access to the U.S. market, the stated goal of the negotiations.
Therefore, your petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to dissolve and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed free trade agreement during a national general election.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FREE TRADE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to table a petition, certified correct pursuant to Standing Order 106, from a large number of British Columbians who are concerned that the Conservative Government had no mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a trade agreement with the U.S. Since the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised in the course of the bilateral trade negotiations that Canadian sovereignty would not be compromised, and since it is now clear that it has been; and since the trade agreement negotiated by the Government threatens Canadian political and economic sovereignty by removing the power of the Government of Canada to effectively control foreign ownership, to develop Canadian energy resources in the best interests of Canadians, or equalize opportunities between the regions, the petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to dissolve and allow the Canadian people to determine the course of Canada in a general election.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FREE TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also have the honour to present a petition signed by many residents of Canada in different provinces indicating their opposition to the
Government on the free trade deal. They believe the Government has no mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a trade arrangement with the U.S. They believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised that in the course of the bilateral trade negotiations Canadian sovereignty would not be compromised. They believe the actual agreement negotiated by the Government threatens the very fabric of Canadian political and economic sovereignty by removing the power of the Canadian Government to effectively control foreign ownership, develop Canadian energy resources in the best interests of the people of Canada, and also prevents us from equalizing opportunities between the regions. They believe the agreement would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future and undermine our ability to build a society distinct from that of the U.S. They also believe the Government did not succeed in acquiring secure access to the U.S. market, which was the key government objective.
Therefore, your petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to dissolve and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed trade agreement through a national general election.

subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO BILL C-33-INDEXATION OF PENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I have a petition which is in order pursuant to Standing Order 106. The petitioners would like to present a common grievance. They say that indexed pensions for all Canadians are essential so that pensioners can protect the value of their pensions from the adverse effects of inflation. They say other employers and Governments recognize the need for indexation and are therefore negotiating and legislating inflation protection for pension benefits.
[DOT] (mo)

subsubtopic: FORT ALBANY FIRST NATION-SAFE SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a duly certified petition pursuant to Standing Order 106. This petition was presented to me during a meeting of the Mushkegowuk Tribal Council in Attawapiskat just a week ago.
The petition is signed by 100 Indian people of the Fort Albany First Nation located on the western coast of James Bay. The band school, Ste. Anne's, has been closed because it is a fire trap. subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO BILL C-55-REFUGEE DETERMINATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to present, for the attention of the House and the Government, three certified petitions. Two of them deal with the refugee legislation, Bill C-55. The petitioners come from the communities of Maple, Scarborough, Rexdale, Brampton, Mississauga, and Toronto. They are petitioning essentially for the elimination of the two stages in the refugee determination system, the first of which we call prescreening and the second, the safe third country concept.
Canadians who have signed these petitions are urging the Government to have a fair and expeditious refugee system, but certainly emphasize the word "fair". Therefore, they urge the Government to eliminate these two stages which essentially build a barrier for any individual who wants to access the refugee determination system in our country.

subsubtopic: CLOSURE OF CANADIAN EMBASSY IN ECUADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the second petition comes from Canadians living in Brampton, Georgetown, Downsview, and Toronto. The petitioners complain about the Government's actions, and in particular those of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), in closing the Canadian Embassy in Equador.
The closing has caused hardship in that people must wait six months to get an appointment at our Embassy in Bogota, Colombia, which is the closest embassy. Canadians on both government and opposition sides of the House have joined in very strong support of the peace process which was initiated over a year ago by President Arias of Costa Rica. We have watched, with some encouragement, the developments. The events of last night and today are major set-backs. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S RIGHTS
speechtext:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to address the needs of the aboriginal people of Canada, including:
(a)	the right to self government
(b)	the provision of adequate shelter, health care and educational facilities,
(c)	basic water and sewage treatment facilities,
(d)	adequate employment and training opportunities, and
(e)	the financial resources to fully develop the economic and human
resources of aboriginal communities.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I presented this motion on behalf of the New Democratic Party today because 1 have found in travels around my riding and other parts of the country that we are creating an increased sense of frustration among our aboriginal Canadians. There has been an increased sense of frustration because many of our first people feel that they are being left out of the government process.
Part of their concern arises from the fact that the meetings that were held between native leaders and our First Ministers failed to include any explanation or definition of aboriginal rights and self-government within our Constitution. The decision in the Meech Lake Accord not to place any extra emphasis on the rights and concerns of our aboriginal people also increased the frustration that exists among them. There is also a concern that government priorities do not address the concerns of native people.
As our motion indicates, we talk not only in terms of housing and shelter, but in terms of education, basic water and

March 17, 1988
Supply
sewage facilities, employment, training opportunities, as well as economic and human development.
The Government did all it could to prevent a UN study of the condition of aboriginal peoples. I believe it did so because it is ashamed of the situation that exists in many parts of our country. Unfortunately, unless someone dies in a fire or someone is beaten, raped or murdered, unless there is a tragedy that appeals to a certain sense within the media, the problems of our native people are not addressed on an ongoing basis.
Those of us with large native communities in our constituencies and those of us who have travelled with committees or on other Elouse business into native communities know the dire straits in which those people live.
This is a very affluent country, but it has a large population that is denied even basic services. There are communities in my riding that have no water supply, no sewage treatment, a school that is condemned and 95 per cent unemployment. There is a basic feeling that the Government is ignoring their concerns.
We are not saying that all the problems are new and can be blamed on the present Government. Many of those problems existed for many years and continue to exist because we have a quickly growing native population.
It is also a situation where the traditional way of life, if not dying out, is certainly unable to sustain the increased population. Unfortunately, the Government and previous Governments, in spite of spending billions of dollars on native concerns, have not spent enough to meet the needs of these people.
It is no surprise to many people in this room that there is a backlog on schools for native people. The projections of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development may deal with building a school on a particular reserve in five or ten years. However, they only take into consideration what the population may be in three years as opposed to what may be needed further in the future. That has been the philosophy of the department, not only under this Government, but with the previous Government as well. As a result, by the time the schools are built in these communities, they already need extra classrooms.
The treatment of young people in these communities is one of the most tragic elements of our dealings with native people. They grow up in dilapidated houses with neither water nor sewage. They go to inadequate schools because less money is spent per capita for the operational costs of the schools than would be the case if they were provincial schools.
In spite of all those disadvantages, these young people are told to compete in our society. Their culture is different from that of the majority of our society. While that may be a benefit in many ways, it makes it very difficult for them to compete in a basically white society. They are expected to live in dilapidated houses with no heat, get up in the morning when it may
be 40 degrees below zero, and attend an overcrowded school. We expect them to be educated in a school system that has less money per capita even though the cost of living is higher because these are remote communities. We expect them to be educated in schools that do not have enough money to stock books in their libraries. They are then expected to go out and face the future.
I am not suggesting that no money is spent on native education, but that not enough money is committed to native education, native housing and its infrastructure for such things as water and sewage.
I brought this motion to the floor of the House today because I believe it is important that members of all Parties have a chance to address these problems. I do not believe we have instant solutions but I believe the House of Commons, and especially the Government, must put much more emphasis on ensuring that the youth in our native communities have a future.
It is not good enough to say that we have spent the entire budget and will only be able to give them a school five years down the road. Those children are growing up now. Each year we delay putting a school into one of these communities makes it that much more difficult for those native people to compete in the future. While it is difficult for us to deal with the problems that many native young people face today and while it is difficult for us to create jobs for a lot of the young adults in native communities, we are just creating a long-term problem for ourselves if we do not guarantee adequate educational facilities and resources for those people who are growing up at this time.
I am often ashamed to be a Canadian as I travel around the native communities in my constituency, not because the Government has not tried but because the commitment is not high enough. Some people will say that the native people can do more for themselves. That is probably true. However, we make it very difficult for them to do so. Anyone who has dealt with the Department of Indian Affairs and Treasury Board knows how hard it is to get something out of those Departments and knows that the process we have to use to have major projects approved is a very difficult and tedious process. A project can be in place two, three or four years before the Government finally gets around to approving it.
There is a great desire among our new native leadership to take control of their own destiny. They recognize that they have to contribute as much as they can to that future. They recognize they have an obligation to build their own future. But we must recognize that they cannot do it without financial resources and without a commitment from the Government.
I find, like many Members of Parliament, that dealing with the Government at the best of times is frustrating, but dealing with the Department of Indian Affairs is the most frustrating process of all. Dealing with the Department of Indian Affairs
March 17, 1988

is an almost impossible task for Members of Parliament, so you can imagine, Mr. Speaker, how difficult it is for a young native leader of 22 to 24 years of age when he or she tries to deal with that bureaucracy. We all know of the political shenanigans that have taken place within the Department of Indian Affairs.
I have often met with Indian leaders who believe they had a commitment from a Minister of Indian Affairs to do something. The Minister of Indian Affairs flies into Winnipeg and meets with some of the native leadership, flies back to Ottawa, and the native leaders believe they have a commitment, only to be told that there is no money in the regional budget or that the programs really do not meet their goals or that some Treasury Board regulation would have to be changed or that this is not what the Minister really meant. We are building more and more frustration. We have made the process so difficult because we do not recognize that these needs have to be met at this time.
Members of all three Parties have spoken in this House in the past about the need to take the decision-making away from Treasury Board and from the Department of Indian Affairs and give it to the bands themselves, the tribal councils and those others who are involved with native economic development within the community. We have had the constitutional conferences on self-government and meetings between the native leadership and government officials in terms of passing over some of those responsibilities. However, the process is taking far too much time. After those First Ministers' meetings with the native leadership, there was still a feeling among native people that there is no commitment in our general society to entrenching aboriginal rights. They went to those meetings, first with former Prime Minister Trudeau chairing and, more recently, with the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) chairing, and each and every time those conferences broke down because the western Premiers refused to budge. These western Premiers had been saying for years that they did not know what Indian self-government and aboriginal rights were all about.
Those Premiers have been coming to conferences for many years. Obviously, they do not spend their time and resources looking at this problem until national television is focused on them. So we are in the situation where these Premiers are saying: "We do not know what it is all about", but how much energy have they really spent trying to resolve the issue of selfgovernment and aboriginal rights? Not that much.
One of the most bitter things for native people is that after all those years of conferences on aboriginal rights, where people could not come to an agreement, especially the western Premiers, the Meech Lake Accord could be agreed to so quickly and that modifications to the Meech Lake Accord could be agreed to just a few weeks later. There are some very important concepts in the Meech Lake Accord. We have all welcomed the inclusion of Quebec into the constitutional family of this country. However, there was a political will at Meech Lake and at the Langevin Block to deal with the
Supply
problem. Very difficult concepts were dealt with quickly, but aboriginal rights take years and years and have still not been resolved.
After the Meech Lake Accord was agreed to, many aboriginal people welcomed Quebec. They expressed their belief that that would also help their cause, as the Prime Minister himself has indicated. But look what happened when the native people asked for simple amendments to the Meech Lake Accord. They asked for a simple guarantee that they will be put on the agenda of the first meeting of the First Ministers', meetings that will now been entrenched in their Constitution to take place on an annual basis.
We have guaranteed in the Meech Lake Accord that fish will be discussed at that meeting. We have guaranteed that the Senate will be discussed. Why not at least show some commitment to the aboriginal people of this country? Why not show the commitment and ensure that at that meeting we will also commence our discussions on aboriginal rights? The Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) have risen in this House and said, "Yes, we will meet sometime on aboriginal rights", but there has been no commitment. I do not believe there is a Premier across this country, or the Prime Minister, for that matter, who would dare say no to the inclusion of the topic of aboriginal rights, along with those other topics of fish and the Senate reform in the next meeting on the Constitution. The failure of the Prime Minister to take the lead, as was suggested by my leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), and at least canvass the Premiers to see if they would agree to have aboriginal rights included at the first conference is a signal that there is no political will involved.
If I can become partisan for a few seconds, I would say that they are also not impressed when they see that the Conservative leader in Manitoba, who was elected leader of that Party for a number of years, now says that he does not know what self-government is all about. Before he was leader of the Party he was a cabinet Minister in the Conservative Government of Manitoba. Yet he does not know what self-government is all about. The last thing the aboriginal people of the country need is another ally of Premier Vander Zalm, Premier Getty, and Premier Devine. Those three by themselves have effectively prevented aboriginal rights from being included in the Constitution.
We are told that if we accept Meech Lake we will have Quebec on side as an ally with respect to some improvements to the definition of aboriginal rights. We do not need a fourth western Premier saying, "No, I do not understand it. It is something that is too complex and I do not want to have it in the Constitution at this time". The failure of the Government to take the political lead when it was possible this spring, when there was a mood in the country to try to resolve a great many problems that existed with our Constitution, may haunt us through 1989 and in the future.

In the few seconds that I have remaining there is one area in the motion with which I would like to deal. I would like to see some commitment from the Government. I have already talked about the problems with general education. However, I have not seen an adequate program for the post-secondary training of native people. There is some training done at the present time, but it is not nearly as comprehensive as it has to be. The number of native people being trained in apprenticeship programs is almost nil. The amount of affirmative action training for native people so that they can enter trades training and apprenticeship training is simply inadequate. In areas in which the provinces try to develop these programs there is a resistance from the Department of Indian Affairs to help pay for them. There is a growing lack of interest on the part of the Department of Employment and Immigration to fund pretrades training and upgrading training for native people.
I spoke earlier about the fact that the educational system guarantees failure for many young native people. Yet later on in their lives when they decide they want to go back to school or want to go to a community college in order to qualify to build their own homes, their own sewer systems, their own water facilities or their own construction programs in their own communities, they are told, "I am sorry, we do not have a program for you". It is time that in all these areas the Government put in place a real program for our native people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member. He made reference in his motion to water and sewage problems. He talked very briefly about these matters and the need for programs in these areas. Can the Hon. Member comment on the federal Government's federal water policy, which also refers to guidelines regarding water quality? These are merely guidelines, they are not legislated. In the water policy it states that the federal Government will continue to consider legislation to ensure the safety of drinking water within areas of federal jurisdiction. Of course, areas of federal jurisdiction include Indian reserves.
Does the Hon. Member see this as a helpful way for Government to stop considering the question but actually proceed to legislation so that we would have some real pressure to clean this matter up?
Has the Hon. Member heard the rumours within the federal Government that the reason we have not proceeded to legislation is that the Minister of Indian Affairs (Mr. McKnight) is afraid of being shown up? Knowing how bad water quality is on Indian reserves and how much money would be required to rectify the situation if there were real legislation with standards and not merely guidelines the federal Government would be required to act. Yet the Minister of Indian Affairs is holding up good legislation because he knows that the consequences would be very severe.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) brings up a very good point. I wish that I had more time when making my speech to deal with water and sewage, because they are real problems in our communities. Each spring as native people go out to get their water, quite often from the nearest lake, there is salmonella poisoning and other bacterial problems which they face.
The Hon. Member is correct when she says that if we were to apply the laws of the land with regard to common safety and with regard to construction codes concerning our reserves, then there would be court case after court case in which the federal Government would be found in contempt of its own laws.
That is why I suspect the Minister of Indian Affairs as well as the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) have always taken the attitude not to legislate what is required in terms of buildings, water and sewage on our reserves. It is not a matter of cruelty by the Government. It is not a matter of neglect. It is just that it does not know that the standards in which our native people are made to live are far beneath those that would be accepted in any other part of our population. It is amazing that the native population has stood it for so long.
If the same situation existed in our towns and cities one could bet that there would be a national outcry. The Journal would have a feature on it. One could bet that the appropriate Minister at the federal or provincial level would promise immediate legislation to solve the problems. However, there is the feeling that if this happens on a reserve then, well, it cannot be helped. It is true that it is very difficult to provide some of those facilities in remote communities. But some reserves are not that remote. Some are next door to white urban communities or right across the river from such communities and they are not receiving these services.
It is true that once provincial Governments are involved quite often services in terms of water, sewage, housing and protection of the law are in existence. There can be a Metis community under provincial jurisdiction, and not just in the Province of Manitoba, such as there is at Cross Lake, which has water and sewage and better housing, and across an imaginary line called the reserve line one finds that there are none of those things.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S RIGHTS
speechtext:
I realize that I do not have time for a long reply on this answer, which is unfortunate. I would like to thank the Member who attended the Standing Committee on Government Operations to hear from the chiefs from Manitoba, including Patsy Turner, the head of the MKO, and also the Chief of the Grand Rapids Band.
At that meeting, the native leadership themselves spoke much more eloquently than I could about the problem. There is not enough money for native housing. There is also a strategy by the Government to take away responsibility for housing from the Department of Indian Affairs and to attempt to make CMHC pick up some of the backlog. This forces people on the reserves to throw up their hands with regard to the housing provided by the Department of Indian Affairs and state that they cannot live in those places because they are terrible. That forces those people, often who do not have an adequate income, to take housing from CMHC.
One of the major problems is that CMHC does not feel that it has a responsibility to provide reserve housing. Many of its rules, regulations, and rent requirements are designed for the cities of Toronto or Winnipeg and are quite appropriate in those communities. The 25-year mortgage is a good indication of this. A 25-year mortgage on a house that will last 40, 50, or 60 years in the City of Toronto is a fairly good investment for many people. But it is not a very good investment for someone who knows that, because of the other problems in the community, the nature of where the houses are built, and the lack of other infrastructure facilities, those houses will disappear or be run down in 10 or 15 years. There are no carpenters available, there are no federal government programs for maintenance, and as a result there is a built-in failure into the system that is in place.

speechtext:
I say that because this evening the Liberal Party opens a policy forum respecting aboriginal peoples and First Nations. I want to say to the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) that in bringing forward this motion the timing is perfect. It fits in very well with the forum which begins this evening. I begin my remarks by thanking the Hon. Member most heartily for using one of the NDP Opposition Days on this important motion.

I also wish to say, Sir, that we will want to have another Opposition Day on the same subject next week after we have heard from aboriginal leaders and groups respecting current concerns, problems, issues, and the agenda for future action.
To a very significant extent the issue of aboriginal rights, of aboriginal title, questions of justice and equity for Canada's indigenous peoples is a question of human rights. In fact, I would consider it to be the oldest yet unresolved question of human rights in the world today.
I always listen with interest and concern in the House of Commons when Hon. Members raise matters of human rights violations around the world, and I always sympathize with them. For example, violations of rights in the Soviet Union, the massive violations against a majority by a vicious white minority in South Africa, violations in Chile, East Timor, Sri Lanka, and those violations against the Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip of the Middle East. All of those are reprehensible and deserve our condemnation and our outrage. But right here on our very own doorstep is one of the major human rights issues in the world today. Yet we in Canada regularly in one way or another attempt to cover it up, disguise it, or gloss over it.
For example, not too long ago the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) circulated to all Canadian embassies around the world the document which tried to give the impression that all is well with the Lubicon Lake Indian people. Yet we know that a way of life there has been destroyed. Disease, poverty, despair, and alcoholism haunt the community. Why would we have the world believe it to be otherwise? The Secretary of State for External Affairs said in the House that he is not responsible for everything that his officials write. But he refused to withdraw the document and he refused to issue an apology to the aboriginal people of Canada.
As well, when the northern Quebec Cree worked hard day and night to get through the Human Rights Commission of the United Nations certain resolutions that were important to the indigenous people of Canada and to the indigenous peoples of the world, Canadian officials were active in lobbying against those resolutions. I have information that they hinted to certain African nations that Canada's aid programs may be reduced; that they hinted to other African nations that our position on apartheid may be less firm if they supported the resolutions as they were drafted.
Here in the House of Commons the Secretary of State for External Affairs would have had us believe that what Canada wanted to do was to broaden and expand those resolutions. In fact, all of the evidence is to the contrary. What was attempted was to water down, postpone, and to soften the resolutions. Why? Because we fear that Canada's record regarding its native peoples may become revealed to the whole world.
When our aboriginal people needed strong support for the maintenance of the fur industry, the trapping of fur being a very important part of the subsistence economy for many

March 17, 1988
Supply
aboriginal people, support from the Canadian Government was, at best, gentle. Embassies and high commissions did not want to get mixed up with the animal rights activists, and they feared facing this lunatic fringe in British and European society. The British Government and the British Parliament have insulted Canada and its indigenous peoples by the act of imposing a labelling regulation on all garments that have been made from furs from trapped animals.
When it comes to foreign aid, which I support of course, we accept the notion that a percentage of the gross national product is the way to go. We never quite reached the United Nations goal, but we always talk about striving for it and aiming to reach it. Yet in Canada the concept of an economic rent to aboriginal people and First Nations, a percentage of the gross national product for housing, education, economic development, community infrastructure, and health, with all of those matters and the policy formulation related to them and the control of those matters being in the hands of aboriginal peoples themselves, all of this is considered to be far out. It is considered to be unacceptable, unworkable, and unachievable.
We continue with the present system of not many changes from year to year. The backlog of Indian housing persists. The program for funding Indian young people in post-secondary institutions is capped. This year, at least 1,000 have been denied access to higher education. Poverty, disease, and a high suicide rate continue to be issues in Indian communities.
Here is the message which the Grand Council of the Cree of northern Quebec delivered to the United Nations Human Rights Commission:
As a group of all the inhabitants of Canada the indigenous peoples are the
poorest, have the worst health, the least education, the highest unemployment,
the most insufficient and dilapidated housing, the highest infant mortality, the
lowest expectation of life.
Of all cabinet portfolios of government, probably the one considered to be the least desirable is that of Indian Affairs. Even National Revenue is preferable. Just imagine, Mr. Speaker, having to go home to your constituency and telling your supporters that the Government of the Prime Minister has just made you the nation's chief tax collector; I think that is one weekend you might want to stay here in Ottawa.
Indian Affairs is still at the bottom, and for very good reasons. Sam Rayburn, a past Speaker of the United States Congress, used to say to new Members of Congress: "If you want to get along here, you had better go along".
If a Minister of Indian Affairs wants to survive, he or she must go along, go along with departmental bureaucrats who basically dislike their clientele. He must go along with his cabinet colleagues who consider the Indian vote to be insignificant and, therefore, why bother putting money or new programs in that direction.
Occasionally in Canada we get a Minister who seems ready to listen, to learn, to understand. When the signal is given, the
Indian people sigh another deep sigh and begin instructing the new Minister all over again. The patience of Canada's aboriginal peoples is simply enormous. When this Minister becomes sympathetic, or better still when he achieves a certain degree of empathy and wants to translate it into concrete action to produce positive results, he is quickly replaced.
The mandate of the most recent Minister of Indian Affairs (Mr. McKnight), as a way of illustration, is to dampen down the expectations, to follow a policy of containment, to control the situation as much as possible, to introduce expenditure reductions wherever they can be done, and to implement the so-called Buffalo Jump report from the Nielsen task force.
The same Minister is given another assignment, as if being Minister of Indian Affairs were not enough in itself. At the same time he is given another assignment which clearly conflicts with his constitutional obligations as Minister of Indian Affairs, his trust responsibilities. He is made Minister of the Western Diversification Program, which, by the way, has within it no component for the assistance of Indian people. This is the Minister who hands out $9.5 million to a Japanese pulp company and, when asked about it in the House of Commons, expresses surprise that the timber to be cut by this pulp company is on land claimed by the Lubicon Indian people. He says he does not know anything about that. It seems to be a rather careless way to handle taxpayers' money.
To help the Minister in the House of Commons, the Government appoints a junior Minister of Indian Affairs. He has not been able to describe even what his duties are. However, I think it is quite obvious that he is expected to be a mouthpiece for the Indian Affairs bureaucracy which, as I said earlier, deeply dislikes its clientele. If one wants to go beyond dislike to outright hostility, then one might become a senior bureaucrat in that Department.
Recently I spoke with a young man who had worked briefly in the Department of Indian Affairs. He said to me, with some puzzlement on his face: "You know, the Indian people actually believe that the Government owes them something". Well, if someone were to come into my house and shove me out into the backyard where I would end up living somewhere between the doghouse and the garbage tins, I too might feel that there was a debt obligation to me.
I know of Indian communities which are located in swamps, where the people have to move from house to house on boardwalks, and if a child were to fall off a boardwalk in the spring of the year, he would disappear forever in the swamp. I know of Indian communities located on flood plains, on the most infertile land imaginable-barren, isolated camps on the fringes of Canadian society. Yet, when these people hunt, when they fish, when they shoot game for their own survival, they are harassed by police and provincial game wardens. Often these people are surrounded by hundreds of thousands of unoccupied square miles of land, yet their land base can never be expanded.
March 17, 1988

The present Government has a policy-no new bands, no new reserves, unless there is a clear obligation imposed upon us. No new bands and no new reserves if the spending of any money is involved. I have a letter before me at the moment concerning the Blackwater Indian Band in northern Ontario. It has been told in a letter signed by the Minister that under current policy for new bands and new reserves the Department can only consider requests for band status where it can be clearly demonstrated that such action will not result in additional funding requirements.
There are Indian people who dwell in very beautiful valleys like the Stein Valley of British Columbia. Even there the exploiters of timber cannot be kept at bay. They must have it all.
What we have today in Canada regarding our aboriginal peoples is a crying shame. They have rights on paper in the Constitution, but it is impossible to get those rights off the paper and into the lives of the people where they are needed, where they live.
Four First Ministers' conferences have failed to give the aboriginal people the rights they are seeking. However, on just one weekend we were able to accommodate the constitutional goals of Quebec. I can never judge a society by deals made among the powerbrokers, by the trade-offs between a monarch and his barons. The way we judge society is how we treat the least powerful elements. I think the whole world ought to realize that this benevolent, this welfare state of Canada, where words like justice, equity and fairness drip off our tongues like hot honey, is among the worst violators of any code of human rights in existence in the world today. The sooner we face up to it, the sooner we cease the cover-up, the excuses, and the better off this nation will be.
The aboriginal people of Canada must have a fair share of our resources, a reasonable percentage of the gross national product, an adequate land base and genuine control of their own lives, real self-determination and not that nonsense being advocated by the Department of Indian Affairs called community-based government, which is nothing more than passing over a few administrative responsibilities to these people with all kinds of strings attached, holding back funds and replacing the old colonial Indian agent with a new yuppie bureaucrat called a monitor.
I support wholeheartedly the motion before the House today. I support any others like it from any source. I would like to end on a note of hope or optimism, but I cannot. I feel nothing but depression, despair and dismay over the entire situation. I do have one brief message for the Government, for this House of Commons and for the nation, that is, until justice is achieved in Canada for aboriginal peoples, this nation cannot and will not be whole. We can never escape our own sorry past, and never would I defend one day of that sorry
Supply
past. Surely we can all try to fashion a better future for the first citizens of this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is a marvellously open-ended question and I thank my colleague for it.
I would add one note which has to do with the concept of aboriginal title. My hon. friend, the Hon. Member from Skeena (Mr. Fulton) is in the House and deeply involved with the subject of aboriginal title. For the Government of Canada and for the Department of Justice to suggest that aboriginal title is no more than a lien, no more than encumbrance or a shadow on the Crown right, is not only insulting but downright stupid. Such a notion from my point of view is based on the outdated concept of the divine right of monarchs. If I read my history correctly, that concept was battled down during the so-called Liberal revolutions of 19th century Europe. It was swept aside then with utter disdain. For some reason, in Canada the concept lives on. It lives on here as a weapon that we continue to use against indigenous peoples to limit the extent of their claims.
In the Province of British Columbia they even consider that aboriginal title has been extinguished, and yet no one can say precisely when this happened or how, nor can they bring forward one single document that would indicate that at any point in history the extinguishment of that title took place. The Nisga people who are visiting Ottawa this week are even unable in that province to get a fishing agreement, although they have accepted, in general, terms proposed by the Government of Canada. The Government backed off on its own terms, because, as best I can conclude, it fears the powerful nonnative fishing lobby in British Columbia.
When the Calder case was before the Supreme Court of Canada, the justices divided equally three for and three against whether extinguishment had taken place in British Columbia. All six of them admitted that aboriginal title under our understanding of British law had existed. Three said it was extinguished and three said it still exists today. I want to say that the Government of Canada and this House of Commons ought to insist that that matter go back to the Supreme Court for final decision. We cannot go on in this deadlocked situation

and leave the aboriginal people of British Columbia bearing the consequences of that deadlock.

Mr. Speaker, as best we have been able to determine, that is those of us who sit on the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs, the budget for Indian Affairs has remained constant, whereas government expenditures have gone up. Almost all departments have received increases in excess of the rate of inflation. The Indian Affairs portfolio has remained flat. It is my impression that the Government has determined that this is one area where effective expenditure control can be successful. I think they have come to this conclusion because we are dealing with a small minority. The cost of meeting the needs outlined in the speech by the Hon. Member for Churchill is enormous. It seems to me that this is an area where there ought to be increases. This is where we ought to be considering more expenditures.
I cannot help but be bothered when the Government talks about wanting to build nuclear-powered submarines to maintain our sovereignty in the North when that sovereignty has been well established by the Inuit people. Why would we want to spend billions on these war toys when we should be investing our money in the first citizens of this country, who delivered so much and made the present prosperity of Canada really possible, if you want to analyse the facts objectively and fairly?

speakeroldname: Mr. Stan Schellenberger (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and comment on this motion. Before I begin, I cannot let the Hon. Member for Cochrane- Superior's (Mr. Penner) last words stand on the record. The facts are entirely the opposite. The budget for Indian and Inuit affairs this year has increased by some 9.7 per cent, almost double the average increase for other departments across the board. That amounts to $181 million more, and the federal budget is now over $2 billion in this field. I am not saying that it is totally adequate, but to say that it has remained the same is just not the way I read the Department's Estimates for the year.
The Hon. Member also said that employees of the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs are not sympathetic to their clientele. I know that each of the Departments concerned can probably find some individuals who fit that category. However, by and large that is just not the case. I would use Mr. Dennis Wallace, the Regional Director in Alberta, as an example. Unfortunately, he just accepted a position in another department. The bands in that province are very unhappy about his leaving. They have called me in great numbers over the last couple of days quite concerned about his move. They came to know him well and realized that he has worked diligently and hard on their problems.
The Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior and I go back a long way in our fight for better conditions for the aboriginal people of Canada. We have worked together for over 16 years on the Standing Committee on Indian and Northern Affairs as it was called, now the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development. When we began, what he said in his speech today was certainly the case. However, to say that after all those years of hard work nothing has really changed surprises me a great deal.
As Chairman of the committee and as a member of the Liberal Government he had successes in making changes in policy and conditions. For example, when we noticed the manner in which European countries were dealing with our fur industry, particularly our aboriginal peoples, we worked together and produced a report that changed the attitude of the departments, the Government, and produced funding to allow the aboriginal people to go to Europe to defend their rights. As well, we have an excellent position in the British Museum, where people can see the manner in which our aboriginal people trap fur. There is much more to do. Hopefully this policy which resulted from the report we produced will continue.
I have made speeches in this House, in opposition and in government, with respect to the conditions of aboriginal people in Canada compared to ordinary Canadians. I can find examples similar to those brought forward by the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) and the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior. I had intended to talk a little bit about that. However, because of the gloomy picture painted here today I want to take a different tack. It is important for
March 17, 1988

us to show that Indian leaders in this country have not been sitting back anticipating that Government is going to solve all their problems. I know for a fact that I have not. By looking at the picture over the last 10 or even 20 years we can see substantial changes in the political and cultural direction in the native community as well as in Canadian society at large.
Canadians are now far more willing to open their hearts to the problems faced by aboriginal Canadians. Budgets have changed to the point that the fastest growing budget in the Government is the Indian and Northern Affairs budget. I will go through these case by case because I think it is important.
Dramatic changes have taken place in housing conditions, education, and in the manner in which the Indian culture is preserved. What I found a little disturbing in the previous two speeches is the lack of balance. I say that not because I am speaking on behalf of the Government but because I believe there is a more balanced picture that can be put before the Canadian people.
I do not believe that the Indian or aboriginal people of this country feel that Government is going to provide them with all their wants, needs and desires. We now have leaders who are going to tell us what they think is important for them in the next decade or into the next century. They do not believe they are totally dependent upon the federal Government. They do not believe the Government is going to provide their shelter and the manner in which it is built. They do not believe the Government is going to provide employment, develop the human and native communities and resources in this country, or provide them with self-government. Absolutely not.
That became very evident when we went through the four national conferences where Indian, Metis and Inuit people communicated directly with the federal and provincial Governments on what they think ought to be in the Constitution with respect to native self-government and native rights. Anyone who knows native people in this country knows that they are not sitting back and waiting for the Government to provide the answers. Indians, Inuit and Metis are more and more taking their future into their own hands. Indian political leaders and ordinary community members are building selfgovernment. The right to self-government is every Canadian's birthright. Unfortunately, it is going to take a little longer for that to be put in place by the Indian people, but they are no exception. It will come and it will be satisfactory to the aboriginal people. I am convinced of that.
Indian entrepreneurs are building businesses and creating employment across this country. We all know that selfgovernment has to have an economic base. You cannot be dependent upon others. That is happening now. Recently I spoke in Alberta as the federal Government assisted new native ventures in that province, contributing upwards of $9 million to the Indian Association of Alberta. They put before us that night numerous examples of successful ventures which have already taken place. They look forward to a great number more as this assistance is being made available. We see
Supply
examples of this across the country from the Sumas Clay Products in Vancouver, which has just opened, to Econobois in Huron Village. We are also seeing native elders taking a larger role again in society as the youth look to them to rebuild the culture, pride and dignity which was so evident in so many communities. The loss of that has been the greatest problem for the youth, resulting in alcoholism, higher death rates, and so on.
Health is more than pills and hospitals. We talked about drinking water. I have not heard that in any way any of our Ministers are holding up legislation with regard to safe drinking water, but we all know that the problem will not be solved by legislation. The important part of health, as I see it, is sound lifestyles.
As an example, in Alkali Lake in British Columbia the chief, council, and elders, viewing a tremendous alcohol problem, took upon themselves the responsibility to solve the problem in their own community. It was not Government or a federal nurse that came in and solved the problem. The community itself said that it had a problem and took the decisions and had the courage to deal with the problem. The results are significant and have been shown to us by the CBC.
Let us not insult aboriginal Canadians by portraying them as passive wards of the state, because they are not. That era of total dependence is behind us. It has taken a long time and there is much more to be done, but I believe and am thankful that it is passing into history.
Nevertheless, the fact remains that Government does have an important role to play in native development. As I have said, the social indicators are still there as enunciated by the two previous speakers. Indians generally do face worse living conditions than other Canadians. As an example, life expectancy for male and female Indians is about 10 years shorter than the Canadian average. Death by suicide is about three times more common among Indians than it is in the general Canadian population. Death from injury and poisoning is four times more common. The employment rate of on-reserve Indians, that is, the percentage of the population 15 years and older which is employed, is around 50 per cent of that of other Canadians. Those facts are undeniable. They represent unfinished business, as all of us in this House acknowledge.
However, we cannot continue to put before the House a litany of negativism. We should take heart in the stunning progress that has occurred over the past generation, and particularly in the last 10 years. I have lived through and witnessed that. The historical perspective is there, as we all know. We have heard it in this House and it bears repeating. However, there has been progress.
Since 1960, Canadian society has opened up to Indian people politically, economically, and socially. Indian leaders have acted with initiative and determination. All Canadians saw that when they viewed the constitutional conferences.

March 17, 1988
Supply
Although they failed actually to write something into the Constitution, their greatest success was in showing all in Canada the capacity and capability of our aboriginal leaders.
Federal government programs and budgets which have benefited aboriginal people have been expanding rapidly and the result has been a generation of advance. The Member for Churchill said that it is frustrating to deal with the Department of Indian Affairs, and it is. As we all go through our ridings, particularly those in the northern parts of the country, we can see the need for change. We come to Ottawa and ask that the changes be made. However, we all recognize that Parliament only votes so much money. Even though the budget of the Department of Indian Affairs is the most rapidly increasing of all budgets, it is still not adequate for all the conditions which we can point out.
Even so, this year we opened six new schools in Manitoba at a construction cost of $55 million. There is a submission before the Treasury Board for $88 million to provide water and sewage programs for five northern flood bands in Manitoba. In 1986-87 the Department of Indian Affairs spent $300 million in actual expenditures in Manitoba. That will increase by $8.3 million this year.
Even with all of those expenditures we will not meet all the needs. However, that does not mean that no advances are taking place. Communities are in fact finally getting the schools and the sewers and water for which they have waited so long.
Until 1961 Indians in Canada did not even have the right to vote in federal elections. Today, only a little over 20 years later, they participate in Canadian political life at all levels. They have served in this House of Commons and in the Senate. They are appointed as our representatives and are, by and large, running their own programs. They have participated directly in four constitutional conferences, as we pointed out ought to be the case in our report on Indian self-government.
In 1960, most Indian communities were still directed by Indian agents. It is hard to believe that it was such a short time ago. These were officials appointed by the federal Government. Today those agents are long gone, they have disappeared. Today band councils chosen directly by their communities administer more than 64 per cent of the funding provided by the federal Government, and that percentage is increasing as rapidly as is possible, as rapidly as the chiefs and councils are willing to accept new responsibilities.
Some bands, including the Cree and Naskapi in northern Quebec and the Sechelt in British Columbia, have sustained their own self-government structures, they are outside the Indian Act. I hope that many others come forward with similar demands to the federal Government. Several more are in the final stages of negotiation.
In the 1960s, Indians had little role in their education. Many students were sent to church-run schools. They were taken away from their homes, and their language and culture were
discouraged. They were cut off from their families and communities. Today there are 243 band-managed schools. The best examples of Indian people taking control of their education are in Manitoba.
There was criticism by the Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) about Government not responding to the demands of Indian students. Although until recent times less than a few hundred made it to post-secondary schools, today some 13,000 Indian students are attending post-secondary schools. Many others are being assisted by training programs of the Government to go to the technical schools. Enrollment since 1981 has increased by over 225 per cent. We are now spending $110 million to assist, in non-returnable grants, Indian students wishing to go to post secondary school. Even with that amount of money some 500 have to wait a year before they can get assistance.
Some 30 per cent of the current housing stock has been built in the last five years alone, and some 35 per cent of that renovated.
The health conditions which we discussed earlier have improved. The situation is much better. I could go on and deal with economic development, but you are pointing out that my time has expired, Mr. Speaker. I just want to conclude by saying that while we can all make the kinds of speeches like those before mine, I believe there has been significant change on the part of Government, aboriginal leadership and Canadians as a whole. I look forward to this increasing in the future.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary indicated that the speeches which preceded him lacked balance. We did not lack balance in our speeches, we only shared the frustration of native constituents and others across the country.
An example of the cause of that frustration was the speech given by the Parliamentary Secretary. It is the same type of speech we heard from the Liberals and their Parliamentary Secretaries when they were in government.
I regret that with two Ministers responsible for Indian Affairs, neither could rearrange his schedule in such a way as to address this issue. I recognize that they have busy schedules, but this is an important matter. Opposition Members made arrangements to speak. The Government received proper notice, and I think an arrangement could have been made.
Today, the Parliamentary Secretary gave us the example of a water and sewage project for five communities in my riding that are affected by a flood agreement. I heard that same commitment in 1984 by the then Liberal Government. It is another example of the frustration that we experience. We are hearing the same promise for the same communities in 1988. They are tired of waiting and tired of hearing politicians make that same promise.
March 17, 1988

The Parliamentary Secretary said that natives want to control their own future and not just rely on Government. I think the speeches from the Opposition made it clear that we understand that.
One way for that to happen in Manitoba is for the federal Government to agree finally to sign the land entitlement treaty. It is an agreement to which the native chiefs have agreed, to which the Province of Manitoba has agreed, and one that the federal Government was negotiating and had agreed to until March, last year. As the Parliamentary Secretary knows, after the tripartite negotiations had taken place and the parties had come to an agreement, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) raised many new questions. I have a copy of that letter from the Minister. It essentially scraps the whole agreement and challenges each and every premise of it.
Land entitlement is fundamental to economic development of the reserves in northern Manitoba. If they do not have that resource they cannot develop their communities as they want. For one year the bands in Manitoba have been trying to get the federal Government to sign this agreement. It has refused to do so. It has refused meetings. There has been no action by the federal Government, other than to say it might discuss it again.
It is that type of unacceptable behaviour which explains the frustration and the type of problem that native people in Manitoba are facing at this time. I want the Parliamentary Secretary to get up and tell me what change took place between January, 1986, and March, 1986, that resulted in the federal Government refusing to sign that land entitlement agreement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Churchill knows that $18.9 million has already been advanced for system design construction of water systems in that area of this province. He is not correct in saying that there has been no action, because that money has already gone out. Let us make sure we have those facts straight.
The same is true for the Member who commented on the Lubicon situation. He said that the Government is basically not doing everything that is being asked by the Lubicon people. I should note that this is the first Government that has decided their claim is valid and has been trying to settle it. It has been negotiating in an attempt to have a reserve delineated in the province. The Government has taken action on longstanding problems.
The Hon. Member stated that the Ministers should be in the House. I know that they wanted to be here and they will be speaking in the debate. We heard of this motion last night at six o'clock. They must attend cabinet meetings that are also important for the aboriginal people of Canada. Today there are on the docket for Cabinet some very important decisions that will deal with aboriginal people. It was impossible for those Ministers to extract themselves from those important
Supply
meetings, after waiting several weeks to get those items on the schedule. I do not think we should leave the impression that they feel this debate is not important enough for them to be here.
I know that I am supposed to be fully briefed on all subjects, but as far as land entitlement is concerned I do not feel adequately briefed about the reasons that there has not been movement in that area. 1 know that further negotiations have been requested, but it would not be fair to ask me for details at this time because I do not have the full information on that area.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly agree with the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) that past administrations do not have much to be proud of when it comes to achievements towards aboriginal rights or solving problems for aboriginal people. I would only expand the list to include the Barrett administration in British Columbia and the Schreyer administration in Manitoba.
Let me return to the Parliamentary Secretary and ask him why he took time in his speech to erect this strawman of passive recipients. I do not remember anything that the Hon. Member for Churchill or I said that suggested that aboriginal people wanted to be passive recipients or wards of the Government. It is quite the contrary.
Does the Parliamentary Secretary not agree that the concept of economic rent and all that is entailed in that involves a direct transfer of payments to be controlled by First Nation Governments themselves, that they become the policy setters and become those who establish their own priorities?
Specifically, I have four questions I want to ask the Parliamentary Secretary. First, does he believe that the capping on post-secondary education assistance will be dropped? Can he tell us that by the time this Parliament comes to an end the current housing backlog will be reduced by even one house? He made reference to the Lubicon Band. Is he convinced that the Lubicon Band will be granted additional land beyond the 25 square miles agreed to in the 1940s when the population was much smaller? Finally, does the Parliamentary Secretary believe that the freeze on the creation of new bands and reserves will be lifted?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is a long list of questions and I will deal with them one by one. I believe $110 million is now being spent for post-secondary education. Some 500 students who applied last year were unable to go to university directly in the year they applied. They will be added to the list this year as first in line. It would be nice in a budget, as I say, that is increasing at the most rapid rate of any budget in the Parliament of Canada, to add additional funds so that everyone can go to school on a grant, non-repayable. That would be nice. I know everyone here would like to see that. However, we have all these other demands which are being put

March 17, 1988
Supply
forward by Members today. The Minister has to make decisions on how he will split the budget up.
There is no decision to make on some of these items, for example, welfare assistance for Indian people. While the amount of money will increase for post-secondary education this year, I do not believe at this time that the "cap", so called, will be removed. Many Canadians cannot go to university in exactly the same year they wish. Many must go out and work for a few years to get sufficient funds to go school. In this case, a very small number of aboriginal people were not able to get funding this year, but they are put first in line on the list for the following year.
With respect to the current housing backlog, we all know that the birth rate in reserves across this country is the highest in the land. Because of Section 31, there are people asking to go back on the reserves and are asking for houses as well, increasing even more the demand for housing. In fact, the budget for Section 31 will be increasing by 116 per cent this year in order to try to meet that need.
I cannot say to the Hon. Member that we will reduce the backlog. What I did point out in my speech is that since 1981, I believe, some 30 per cent of the housing on reserves is new housing, and some 35 per cent of the housing since 1981 has been reconditioned. Budgets have increased. I think two or three years ago we increased the budget by some $50 million. That has remained in the budget in the last number of years. Again, work has been done to attempt to deal with this very serious problem.
As far as the Lubicon band is concerned, the Member himself mentioned the difficulties we have with the Constitution and provincial lands being set aside. The Government, as I understand its process, is asking for, without prejudice, a reserve to be set aside. Then negotiations will take place for additional land, or services, depending on how the negotiations go. I think that is a reasonable position to put forward. The federal Government is taking the lead finally in this area.
While discussions do not always go in the manner we wish between the band, the province and the federal Government, at least progress is being made. People are talking and negotiating. In the last month or so an advancement has been put forward and it looks as though it might be a fruitful advance.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on the motion of the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) seconded by the Hon. Member for the Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin). I think it only appropriate to begin by reading Part II, Section 35(1) of Canada's Constitution with respect to the rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada. It reads:
The existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada
are hereby recognized and affirmed.
I think I can demonstrate in the moments provided to me that the Government of Canada is not living up to the Constitution of this country.
If one is to take the opportunity, as I have, to look at the budget of aboriginal affairs over the last 10 years, or even over the last four years, one can see the essential increase in the elements. The Parliamentary Secretary talked about an increase greater than that of other departments in the Government. The reason there is any increase at all is in relation to a ruling of the United Nations not by any sudden burst of interest by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) or by his Cabinet. It was the Lovelace ruling on Section 12(l)(b) with respect to sexual discrimination that has brought about the essential increase in the budget.
One can go through the essential elements of the budget and demonstrate that, which I intend to do this afternoon. It is clear beyond reasonable doubt that the Government of Canada is intentionally implementing Buffalo Jump in the 1980s, the famous document by the former Deputy Prime Minister, the Hon. Erik Nielsen from the Yukon. He and Mr. Collison developed a document on how to bring about the forced assimilation of the aboriginal people of Canada. The constitutional route has been closed off. Funding has been closed off for resource development impact studies. Funding for litigation has been closed off, except at the appeal level.
I intend to demonstrate this afternoon when I carry on with my remarks why all the people of Canada should be concerned regardless of their political persuasion. I think we can demonstrate, as the Hon. Member for Churchill and the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) have done, and the Hon. Member for the Yukon will do this afternoon, and adequately and properly sustain an argument, that the Government of Canada is presently launched on a process of forced assimilation. Certainly, if one speaks to the aboriginal
March 17, 1988

leaders, it can only be described as bare-faced cultural genocide. I intend, with your agreement, Mr. Speaker, to carry on the bulk of my remarks immediately following Question Period at three o'clock.

subsubtopic: ATTEMPT TO REMOVE SUBJECT FROM SCHOOL CURRICULUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the Conservative Government is busy tarnishing the reputation of the Canadian Sikh community thanks to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), the Minister's Department is now extending this dangerous game to Canadians of Armenian descent.
An Assistant Deputy Minister from the Minister's Department has written to the Ottawa Board of Education requesting that the subject of the Armenian genocide not be part of the school curriculum because, in the Government's eyes, the genocide did not occur, and the course would impact negatively on the Government of Turkey. Not only did the Government break its campaign promise of July 23, 1984, of recognizing and condemning the Armenian genocide before the United Nations, but the Conservatives are attempting to rewrite history as well.
In addition, like the Sikh issue, the Government will go to the ends of the earth to please foreign Governments, even if that means hurting and demeaning Canadian citizens here at home.
I call upon the Minister and the Government to retract and immediately to recall this letter to the Ottawa Board of Education, to refrain from attempting to hide certain human rights violations while championing others, and immediately to stop being coerced into writing foreign policy which may please the world and foreign Governments but which is completely unacceptable for domestic consumption here at home.
This is no longer an isolated incident, it is a-
