subtopic: CONCERNS OF PERSONS AGED BETWEEN 40 AND 55 YEARS
CONCERNS OF PERSONS AGED BETWEEN 40 AND 55 YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had a meeting with people in the 40-55-year age group who are very disappointed in the Conservative Government because they would have liked the Government to start thinking about their needs and concerns.
They would have liked the Government to introduce genuine pension reforms, provide for broader participation in private pension plans, establish a form of indexation for private pension plans, enable three million women working in the home in Canada to contribute to the Quebec Pension Plan and the Canada Pension Plan, provide for increased portability of private pension plans, maintain early retirement programs, and eliminate the discrimination against early retirees that consists in cutting off their unemployment insurance benefits.
I have almost finished, Mr. Speaker. I want to give these people the assurance that on April 15 and 16, at the Liberal Party's convention in Quebec City, we intend to discuss these issues, and on March 26 as well, at the Montreal East Seminar.

Mr. Speaker, the Biannual Arctic Winter Games this year are being successfully held in Fairbanks, Alaska. A thousand young athletes from the Northwest Territories, the Yukon, Alaska, and a contingent from northern Alberta are competing for the Golden Ulus. In the past northern Quebec has participated. We look forward to Greenland joining in to give the Games an even more international flavour.
This showcase of northern sport, culture, and international friendship touches on nearly everyone who lives in the North. It is a continuing success and fully worthy of the $250,000 contribution by the Government of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to alert the House to a tragedy that may be taking place as we speak. This week there are several Conservative Members of Parliament in the Yukon trying to sell the trade deal. If that

March 17, 1988
is not tragedy enough, I certainly hope that they are not travelling by car or we may hear that some of our esteemed colleagues are languishing in a three-foot pothole on the Alaska Highway.
The Alaska Highway, a federal highway, is the only transportation link to the south. Since 1982 there has been a 42 per cent cut in maintenance and operating expenditures. Staff has been cut by half.
The Minister of Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) said that the North must become more self-sufficient if we are to gain constitutional development. At the same time the Government is cutting back on major essential services such as this highway.
The pleas of the Yukon Government, local municipalities, local business, and hundreds of residents who live along this highway have gone unheeded by the Government.
I call on the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes), the Minister of Transportation (Mr. Crosbie), and the Minister of Northern Development to restore funding now before new meaning is given to the term "spring breakup".

subtopic: WILFUL SPREAD OF AIDS DISEASE-CALL FOR AMENDMENT
WILFUL SPREAD OF AIDS DISEASE-CALL FOR AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to offer my congratulations to the Ottawa Police Force on its decision to release the photograph of a man who donated AIDS contaminated blood.
AIDS is a terrible disease which must be dealt with by harsh measures, if we are to protect all Canadians. Any individual who would knowingly put others at risk loses the right to privacy.
Photographs should be released, nation-wide if necessary. Photographs will act as a warning to the public that these individuals are a health hazard.
I do not propose to invade the privacy of those carrying the AIDS antibody. Only those individuals who knowingly spread this disease, lacking thought for the innocent, should be subject to this kind of scrutiny.
In addition, I would like to urge the Government to amend the Criminal Code to deal with the wilful spread of AIDS. The common nuisance charge currently being used does not adequately address this issue.

subtopic: ATTEMPT TO REMOVE SUBJECT FROM SCHOOL CURRICULUM
ATTEMPT TO REMOVE SUBJECT FROM SCHOOL CURRICULUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak out against the new policy of the Department of External Affairs of denying the Armenian genocide, and requesting the Ottawa Board of Education to deny it also. It is reported that the Board of Education is being asked to withdraw student course materials about the Armenian genocide. The reasons given by the Department of External Affairs are because of a request from Turkey that it gives Turkey a bad image, and because of millions of dollars of possible Canadian trade with Turkey.
This is a despicable Canadian policy which is beneath contempt in a free and democratic country like ours. The Armenian genocide is a tragic historical fact, whether or not the Governments of Turkey and Canada like it. Our Government should be protecting Canadians and Canadian institutions like the Ottawa Board of Education from the pressures of foreign Governments. Lately, our Government has made itself the enforcer of foreign Governments like Turkey, and India which wants to constrain the Sikh community groups and is getting help from the Department of External Affairs to do so.
I urge the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to get a Secretary of State for External Affairs who values free speech in Canada and who respects multiculturalism.

subtopic: AWARENESS OF ACCESS FOR THE HANDICAPPED WEEK
AWARENESS OF ACCESS FOR THE HANDICAPPED WEEK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) is involved in preparations for the National Access Awareness Week for disabled persons, from May 29 to June 4, 1988, which is intended to draw the public's attention to the needs of the disabled.
The objective is to create "Five Star" communities where five basic services, namely, accommodation, employment, transportation, recreation and education will be accessible to everyone.
Each community will assess its ability to provide all members of the community with access to these services and will be encouraged to make improvements before next year's Week in order to get a better score.
During the same Week, the Secretary of State will sponsor a seminar on the concerns of disabled women.
Mr. Speaker, municipal authorities must be properly prepared for this event.
March 17, 1988

subtopic: IRRADIATION OF FOOD-PRACTICE BANNED BY UNITED KINGDOM
IRRADIATION OF FOOD-PRACTICE BANNED BY UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House will recall that the Government rejected the recommendations of the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs to stop the irradiation of food in Canada. The committee feared abuse of this technology since there is no way of identifying whether or not food has or has not been irradiated, or to know the dosage.
Recently the United Kingdom decided it is necessary to ban irradiated foods. What stirred British politicians to action? Freshwater shrimp which had been imported to the United Kingdom and cold stored for two months was sent to the Netherlands to be irradiated to freshen it for reintroduction to the British market.
Such activities are illegal and against the guidelines established by WHO, FAO, and IAEA, but there is no way of monitoring or testing to see if the guidelines have been met or breached. Surely the safest route is to refrain from the use of irradiation for food processing until the questions raised by the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs are answered.

Mr. Speaker, in light of the current controversy over half-way houses in this country, I wish to commend the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) for his response to the Pepino Report. The Minister has already taken action, and has also accepted the 32 recommendations made by the inquiry board, but still much has to be done to ensure the protection of society as well as proper transition for halfway house residents.
This type of leadership is what Canadians desire, especially in the area of corrections. The Solicitor General is acting with justice and compassion on an issue that is very sensitive today. 1 encourage the Minister to make sure that public safety will continue to be foremost in his actions.
As we continue to search for right answers and just solutions, we must pursue action that is beneficial to all Canadians. The Solicitor General has heard the pleas of Canadians and is responding.

Mr. Speaker, it was with great sorrow that we learned of the decease of Senator Yvette Rousseau last night. I would like to recall, for the benefit of all Members, the considerable accomplishments of Mrs. Rousseau, not only as a Senator, but also in her family and professional life. She raised eight children. She focussed all her energies on defending women's rights, especially within the labour confederations. She chaired the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women and published a book on the circumstances of women who worked the night shift in factories. She was dedicated to defending the status of women in Canada and to the emancipation of her sex.
Speaking on behalf of my colleagues in Quebec and of all Members of this House, I wish to extend our sincere condolences to Mrs. Rousseau's family, to her children.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FEDERAL ACTIONS TO ASSIST BRITISH COLUMBIA
FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FEDERAL ACTIONS TO ASSIST BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not unusual in Canada for provincial Governments to grumble about how much money or how many contracts they receive from the federal Government. It has become kind of a national sport and, as we have seen this week, British Columbia is no exception.
However, I would ask the people of British Columbia to consider that the good news this Government has brought for B.C. cannot be measured in grants or contracts alone, although those have been ample, but in actions such as keeping our West Coast ports open, eliminating the container clause, promoting an international banking centre, free trade, increased foreign investment, and record lumber and paper exports.
Perhaps upon reflection Premier Vander Zalm might like to reconfirm what he said to our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) last fall at the First Ministers' meeting: "You have shown a greater desire to strive for fairness and equality than any of your predecessors".
That is the hallmark of this Government-to treat all regions with fairness and all Canadians as first-class.

March 17, 1988

Mr. Speaker, as another federal election draws near, the Bobbsey Twins of Bay Street can be seen at play again. Their latest game concerns encouragement of a Canadian deep-sea fleet.
This is actually a very old game. When successive Liberal Governments had failed to take action on a Canadian deep-sea fleet, the last Liberal Minister of Transport decided to appoint a task force to give it another kick. He took care, however, to load the task force with people concerned about cheap shipping rates.
The last Liberal Minister also appointed the task force in April, 1984, more than four years after the previous election. The task force, quite naturally, did not report until June, 1985.
The present Conservative Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) has not waited quite as long. His Government is only 3.5 years old. He is excited about the possibility of tax exemptions for those owning and working Canadian-owned and crewed vessels. However, shipping is a service industry and he seeks the reaction of the shippers.
The Minister of Transport has called for a report from the industry and the government Department within six months. Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that a general election will occur before the report is released? Truly, plus fa change, plus c'est la meme chose!

maintopic: GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-ACCEPTANCE OF CAIRNS GROUP FORMULA URGED

maintopic: GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-ACCEPTANCE OF CAIRNS GROUP FORMULA URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to accompany Canada's Grains Minister to the recent meeting of the Cairns Group in Argentina.
Canada is a leader in this group of countries which has placed agriculture at the top of the agenda in the latest GATT round. It is crucial to maintain the momentum to end trade distorting behaviour in farming. The European Economic Community, the United States, and Japan must be persuaded to accept the Cairns Group formula for restoring order to agricultural trade.
Over the past seven years world-wide agricultural subsidies have increased from $100 billion to approximately $300 billion. As subsidies rise, more of Canada's farm families are placed in jeopardy.
The Government will continue to pursue the agricultural trade issue in the present multilateral trade negotiations. We
believe that the future of prairie farmers is too important for us ever to stop pushing.

subtopic: PRIVATIZATION OF POST OFFICE IN MORRIN, ALTA.
PRIVATIZATION OF POST OFFICE IN MORRIN, ALTA.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I should like to read to the House a letter which I received from a concerned citizen of Morrin, Alberta. It reads:
At a recent public meeting held in the Morrin Community Flail on February 11, Canada Post officials advised us that our local post office is going to be privatized because of the upcoming retirement of our postmaster.
We were led to believe from the Canada Post officials at our meeting that it costs more for door to door service in the city than it does-to have our rural post office.
Not only is Canada Post closing rural post offices but it is also not delivering the mail door to door. The people in rural Canada believed that it was closing the rural post offices because it was delivering mail in the cities, but it is not.
Why is Canada Post pitting Canadians against each other, rural Canadians against urban Canadians?
Canada Post is not living up to its mandate of delivering mail, giving good service. With labour management relations the way they are, how can Canada Post deliver the mail? Is the Minister going to do something once and for all?

Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) made his calculations on the provincial share of stabilization payments for the 1985 potato crop for Prince Edward Islanders, he excluded the 104,703 metric tonnes of potatoes put through the diversion program for Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick potatoes. This is wrong.
These calculations should have been made on the total amount of potato production from Prince Edward Island, which would have been 613,502 metric tonnes. The Minister, by using those figures, has shortchanged the farmers of Prince Edward Island $800,000. In other words, the per acre payment under the stabilization program for the 1985 crop year will now be paid out at $56.13 an acre. If the proper calculations had been made, Prince Edward Island farmers should receive something in the order of $70 an acre. I do not think the situation is fair, and I hope that the Minister of Agriculture
March 17, 1988

will reconsider the stabilization program for 1985 and get on with the job of getting the cheques out and correcting the inequity.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: CENTRAL AMERICA-HOSTILITIES ON NICARAGUA-HONDURAS BORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question today for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
In recent days and weeks we have had news of trouble all over the world. We have had the senseless tragic slaying at the funeral in Belfast, the problem of the control of Panama, the conflict in the Middle East, and the oppression in South Africa.
I want to ask the Minister specifically today about the situation as he sees it in Central America. I know that the Minister met last evening with members of the special House committee who desire to advance, as they can, the peace process in Central America. Does the Minister have any further information that he feels he can share today with Members of the House? Would he give us the Government's current information about the state of hostilities on the Nicaragua-Honduras border? What action has the Government of Canada taken to help reduce the level of those hostilities?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CENTRAL AMERICA-HOSTILITIES ON NICARAGUA-HONDURAS BORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate particularly the very careful tone in which that question was put, and I will provide all of the information that is available to me.
I think it would be agreed by all in this House that developments recently in Central America are regrettable and are not at all helpful to the peace process that Canada supports and which an all-Party committee of the House will be visiting the region to help advance.
It is not clear what has happened on the border between Honduras and Nicaragua. It is not clear whether there were troop incursions of the kind that had first been reported or whether there had been the equally serious threat of significant shelling. What is clear is that those events and the response to them are moving us back into a military situation and away from the peace process.
Our very able Ambassador, Stan Gooch, was in Managua yesterday. He was in Tegucigalpa, Honduras, today. We are seeking information from him, and I will certainly report to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition and to other interested Members of the House as soon as we have it.
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Secretary of State for External Affairs for that answer, and I would like to pursue it a bit.
Has the Canadian Government been in touch with the Government of Nicaragua, the Government of Honduras and, indeed, the Government of the United States? What position does our Government take with respect to the deployment today of American troops to Honduras? Would the Minister advise us whether he or the Prime Minister have been in touch with President Arias of Costa Rica or any other of the leading advocates of the Central American peace plan? Would he advise us-he mentioned his Ambassador-what instructions he has given to his special Ambassador to Central America as to what action he should undertake?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORTED DEPLOYMENT OF UNITED STATES TROOPS TO HONDURAS

Mr. Speaker, we have been in touch with the three Governments mentioned, those of Nicaragua, Honduras, and the U.S., seeking information on this matter. We are seeking that information and certainly intend to use again all of Canada's influence to encourage the peace process.
We have not been in touch recently with President Arias, although that is a very useful suggestion and may well be a contact that would be quite helpful to the process for Canada to make quickly.

Does the Minister intend to raise the matter at the United Nations in a constructive attempt to support a reduction in military operations between Honduras and Nicaragua, and in Central America? subsubtopic: ATTEMPT TO EXCLUDE SUBJECT FROM SCHOOL CURRICULUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. A few weeks ago the Minister wrote a letter condemning Canadian Sikh organizations in order to preserve the Government's good relations with India. Yesterday a senior official in the Department of External Affairs stated in a letter to the Ottawa Board of Education that the Board is wrong to call the documented massacre of hundreds of thousands of Armenians by the Ottoman Empire genocide. The extraordinary reason given was that this would have "a negative impact on Canada-Turkish relations", and that it would "jeopardize millions of dollars" in trade contracts."
I ask the Minister on behalf of Canadians of Armenian origin, is it the policy of the Government to ignore the documented historical reality of the Armenian genocide in order to preserve good trading relations with Turkey?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ATTEMPT TO EXCLUDE SUBJECT FROM SCHOOL CURRICULUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the short and direct answer to that question is no. The Hon. Member, inadvertently I am sure, misconstrued and misrepresented the letter which I sent to various Premiers with regard to the activities of three organizations representing a tiny minority of the Sikh population of Canada.
With regard to the letter to which he referred, I first saw this letter shortly after noon today after my attention had been drawn to news reports in The Ottawa Citizen. The letter
should not have been sent. This is a world in which people make mistakes, and it was a mistake to send this letter.
If there are to be representations on behalf of an embassy in Canada regarding its particular interests to a Canadian body, those representations should be made directly by the embassy. The Department of External Affairs should not have been involved.
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to question the Minister's statement that he heard about the letter only a few moments ago.
However, I would like to ask the Minister, since we are not talking about some third secretary but about an assistant-deputy minister responsible for the Common Market, if I am not mistaken, is the Minister prepared to rise in his seat and apologize on behalf of the Government to the Armenian community in Canada for the kind of treatment it received from a senior official, especially when we realize that in 1985, Canada voted on and supported a resolution to recognize the Armenian genocide as such, and when we realized that the Conservative Party promised in its election platform to give public recognition of this fact-
Is the Minister prepared, here and now, to apologize to the Armenian community in Canada for the action taken by a senior official in his Government?
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, as far as the basic issue is concerned, the position of the Government of Canada is well known and it has been stated in this House.

subsubtopic: CENTRAL AMERICA-NICARAGUA-UNITED STATES SUPPORT FOR CONTRA FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs which follows up on questions which the Minister was answering earlier.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs will know, Nobel Peace Prize winner President Arias said recently, with regard to American military support for the Contras, that this is "the main problem and not the solution" to the problems in the area.
March 17, 1988

Today an American politician said that recent action by the Reagan administration is "an irresponsible involvement of American troops in the conflict in Central America and an unwise escalation of tension in that region".
Does the Secretary of State for External Affairs agree with both of those opinions?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CENTRAL AMERICA-NICARAGUA-UNITED STATES SUPPORT FOR CONTRA FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, part of the strength of the Arias plan has been the very significant personal leadership that has been shown by President Arias and his determination to be evenhanded and frank in his references to the activities not only of the United States but also the influence of the Soviet Union in that region.
It is the policy and the practice of the Government, and I believe this is a matter on which there is all-Party agreement, actively to encourage President Arias and his Government.
With regard to the American action, as I indicated earlier, we do not have available to us sufficient information as to what is happening along the border between Nicaragua and Honduras to be able to cast a judgment of the kind apparently made by a public figure in the United States.

Mr. Speaker, I commend the Secretary of State for External Affairs in general for his approach to the problems which have emerged in the region. However, with respect, I would ask him to be a little more specific in the present circumstance.
Whatever the precise nature of the border problem, there have been attacks and violation of international law by Honduras from Contras coming into Nicaragua. There has, in turn, been reciprocal, if you like, chasing of Contra troops back over the border. There have been a number of incidents.
However, what we are now talking about is superpower involvement, whether by the Soviet Union in this region at times in the past, or elsewhere. Today we are talking about an escalation of superpower involvement by the United States.
Will the Minister be clear with the House about that? Does he think that this recent action by the United States is counterproductive and a step toward further military approaches to a solution rather than peaceful ones? If he does believe that, as I am inclined to think he does, will he say so publicly?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to be as clear as I can on the basis of information I have available to me now, what is and has been happening in recent days in Central America is highly counterproductive. It runs against the success of the Arias Plan which is the best possibility for peace in the region.
Oral Questions
I cannot judge, on the basis of the information available to me at this stage, the nature or the motivation of the action by the United States Government. I do not think anyone in this country can do so on the basis of the information we have available now.
There has been a change in the information coming to us regarding what has been occurring on the border. If we have information which would lead us to be specifically critical of anyone, including the United States, I will certainly be specifically critical of any Government that is taking an unusual role in creating problems for the Arias Peace Plan in that region.

Regrettably, one has to say that the usual role of the Reagan administration, to make a distinction between that and the administrations of others in the region, has been to support military action. The whole world knows that President Reagan recently lost an important vote in the U.S. Congress where the American Congress made it clear that it does not favour military intervention.

subsubtopic: DUTY REMISSION ASSISTANCE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Yesterday, in response to a question I raised concerning the position taken by the clothing industry of Canada that they had been given an offer of a $200 million relief package to compensate for the damage that would be done by the proposed trade agreement with the United States, the Minister denied that any such discussions had taken place.
I have a copy of minutes which include as participants at the meeting, the Deputy Minister of Trade, senior officials from the Department of Finance and the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, and in which the industrial leaders point

March 17, 1988
Oral Questions
out that the industry would suffer job losses from 35,000 to 50,000 unless remedial action is taken.
The minutes go on to say that the duty remission program commitment from Ministers has been $100 million for the apparel industry, $50 million to the apparel industry for garments, and $50 million to the textile industry. I suggest that is fairly strong evidence that the Government has been making a specific offer to the industry to provide for compensation for the major losses it will suffer as a result of the trade agreement. Why is the Government reneging on this commitment?

subsubtopic: DUTY REMISSION ASSISTANCE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been no reneging on any commitment. What we have indicated to the industries, both the clothing and textile industries, is that we are prepared to discuss with them a package of initiatives that will help them adjust to the free trade environment. The Hon. Member should know that a substantial duty remission scheme for the clothing industry has the effect of bringing in low cost products to Canada which are competitive with the Canadian textile industry. It is for that reason that there has to be a balance between the various sectors of the apparel industry and the textile industry so that an action that might help one segment of the industry does not undermine the competitive position of another segment of the industry.
That is the balance we have been trying to find in the consultations that we have been having with the various segments of the industry. As I have indicated in the past, we are coming close to a resolution of this and I believe we should be able to make an announcement on it shortly.

subtopic: EFFECT OF CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
EFFECT OF CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is the Government of Canada that has put both the textile and clothing industries in the dilemma they face by signing an agreement with the United States that puts them at a disadvantage. It is up to the Government to find a solution based upon a minimum commitment.
Yesterday two garment manufacturers in the city of Winnipeg, Gemini and Tan Jay, both said they would be forced to close their plants and move south to the United States because of the trade agreement unless they get the minimum assistance of the $200 million package that was originally offered, as these minutes clearly prove. Will the Government stick to its compensation package that will amount to a minimum of $200 million so that those plants in the city of Winnipeg will not have to close down and the workers be without jobs?

subtopic: EFFECT OF CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I think there are some great opportunities for both those companies as a result of the free trade agreement. I believe those two gentlemen would acknowledge that they have some
very good opportunities to take advantage of as that market opens up into the United States.
They are businessmen and obviously are speaking from a certain degree of self interest because a very high duty remission scheme can help their as two companies. At the same time as we help them we do not want to undermine the textile industry which is represented by a number of colleagues in this House. There are textile manufacturers in Winnipeg as well. There are textile manufacturers in Montreal, Toronto, and Vancouver. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition should be concerned about this.
We do not want to undermine the textile industry of this country.

subtopic: EFFECT OF CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: You signed the agreement. You caused the problem.

subtopic: EFFECT OF CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: The Hon. Member says that I signed the agreement. I did sign the agreement. Not only did I not cause a problem, I created great opportunities. This Government has created great opportunities for that industry.

Mr. Speaker, we learned today that the United States Department of Agriculture forecasts that soon 60 per cent of American wheat exports will be subsidized and that the American share of the world market will have gone from 30 per cent to 41 per cent. Much of this will have been accomplished by big sales to the Soviet Union and China, traditional Canadian markets, through the use of the Export Enhancement Subsidy Program.
My question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who told me and other Members of the House in October, 1987, that in his view the American use of this Export Enhancement Subsidy Program was inconsistent with the spirit of the free trade agreement. What is the Government prepared to do, given the increasingly effective use of this program by the Americans to undermine Canadian sales in traditional Canadian markets? What is it prepared to do about this for the sake of Canadian farmers?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me make two or three points in responding to the question. First, the figures to which the Hon. Member referred are a recommendation which was made by the subcommittee, not a decision by American officials. Second, the implications for Canada are very clear, and demonstrate the continuing importance of moving toward freer liberal trade agreements amongst all nations of the world, including Canada and the United States.
March 17, 1988

Third, and most important, the Hon. Member should recognize the tremendous success of the Canadian Wheat Board which, in the face of the Export Enhancement Program, has succeeded in increasing Canadian exports from 19 per cent to 23 per cent during the course of the last year.

Mr. Speaker, I would hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs would see his way clear to respond on behalf of the Government of Canada. After all, it was he who said in this House that it was inconsistent with the trade agreement.
The Canadian Wheat Board may well be doing the good job the Member says it is, but the Canadian Wheat Board should not have to work in spite of efforts by Americans to do what they are doing with the Export Enhancement Subsidy Program. How long is the Canadian Government going to put up with this kind of action by the Americans? Are we just going to continue to roll over and play dead? Or is the Secretary of State for External Affairs going to get up and say something on behalf of Canada and Canadian farmers?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could not be more eloquent or more effective than my colleague, the Hon. Member for Brandon- Souris, who has put on the record the context in which these matters have to be seen.
The Member knows the complexity of the problem. He also knows, because we have discussed it, that senior Ministers in the United States administration are as unhappy about this program as we are. He will know that it was mounted in the context of a conflict between the European Community and the United States, in which Canada is a potential principal victim. He will also know that, as a result of representations made by this Government and others, most recently by the Prime Minister when he met with Jacques Delors, the President of the European Commission, there has at last been some movement back in some of the subsidy programs of the European Community.
That does not provide us with the immediate relief we need now, but, as my colleague, the Member for Brandon-Souris, (Mr. Clark), has just indicated, the actions and effectiveness of the Canadian Wheat Board mean that Canada is continuing to sell effectively and aggressively abroad while we are making progress in trying to iessen the consequences of the conflict between the European Community and the United States on agriculture.

On the matter of the Supreme Court decision, as I have said on other issues, the Government of Canada obviously expects the provinces to obey the law. As has been stated before, I think that is only as far as I can go until the federal Government comes in with other legislation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are fortunate in today's debate to have with us in the gallery a very notorious Canadian and British Columbian, Mr. Frank Calder, who served with distinction as the first Indian to be elected to a
legislature in Canada. He was elected in 1949 and served with distinction for more than 30 years.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S RIGHTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S RIGHTS
speechtext:
Many Canadians will know that Mr. Calder brought before the Supreme Court of Canada the first major landmark decision on aboriginal title, which resulted in a tie decision before the Supreme Court of Canada in 1972.
I wish to spend a moment talking about part of the history of British Columbia which brought about the remarkable Calder case and a reversal of federal government movement in terms of comprehensive claims.
As some Members of the House will know, the first contact between the Nisga people, most aboriginal people in British Columbia, and the non-native global population was when Captain Vancouver came with his expedition to Observatory Inlet and Salmon Cove and contacted the Nisga at that time.
In looking back, it is interesting to note that in 1858 the Hudson's Bay Company conducted for the colony of British Columbia what could be described as a census of some sort. They could very easily come up with the number of non-native people in British Columbia; there were 400 whites in Victoria at the time. They estimated that there were 63,000 Indians in British Columbia. Recently historians have pointed out that there may well have been in the neighbourhood of 400,000 Indian people living on the coast of British Columbia and in the Pacific northwest prior to contact. Many people who are here today will know that it was as a result of smallpox that more than 90 per cent of the aboriginal people in British Columbia were decimated during the 1860s and 1870s.
In British Columbia the aboriginal population enormously outnumbered the non-native population according to Hudson's Bay Company records, of 63,000 to 400 only one century ago, and we found that that was the case throughout most of Canada. It was through very important alliances that were formed that this country came into being and successfully fought the War of 1812 and other major sovereign battles in which this nation was involved over the last several centuries.
The shoe is now on the other foot. There are now 25 million Canadians. One need only look at the documents tabled by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) to see how things have changed from an enormous native population and important military and economic alliances for the fur trade and for the forest and mining industries. We now find the non-native population enormously outnumbering the native population.
According to government records, as of December, 1986, there were 387,829 status Indian and Inuit in Canada. During 1986, 10,844 more were reinstated as a result of pressure brought on Canada by the United Nations via the Lovelace case to change Section 12(l)(b) of the Indian Act, which had sexually discriminated against Indian women for a better part of the century. Between June, 1985 and May, 1987, 24,708
March 17, 1988

individuals were reinstated, but only $25 million was provided, about $1,000 per person, to assist those who were returning to their home communities. The Government estimated that some
56.000	would be reinstated, but we know that more than
100.000	have applied so far and only half have been properly reinstated.
Earlier today we heard the Minister's Parliamentary Secretary say that if one looks at the social indicators of the plight of the aboriginal people of Canada, every Canadian must shudder to realize that aboriginal people face the highest infant mortality rate in Canada; the lowest life expectancy in Canada, some 10 years less than any other minority; the highest rate of unemployment, the highest rate of suicide, and the lowest standard of living, to name but a few of the social indicators.
There are 592 bands in Canada ranging from populations as small as 2 to an excess of 11,000 members. There are 2,263 separate parcels of land with a burgeoning population of whom a full two-thirds are under the age of 25 years.
The Government of Canada has launched an attack which we have not seen since the White Paper of Jean Chretien back in 1971. This Government has gone further, as we learned with the Buffalo Jump of the 1980s, the document prepared by Erik Nielsen in his task force study on how to assimilate and eliminate aboriginal people in Canada.
We have now seen the Prime Minister close off the constitutional route. In my view he intentionally failed. We can discover how far the Government is prepared to go in blocking constitutional evolution and devolution by simply looking at the Estimates which were tabled just a few weeks ago by the Minister. If one looks under policy and the Constitution, we find a cut of 30 per cent in funds under Section 2-31 of the Estimates. Staff has been cut in that area by two-thirds since 1986. On self-government negotiations there has been a cut of 25 per cent, and the staff has been cut by 50 per cent since last year.
These kinds of cuts are absolutely indefensible. When I started speaking just before one o'clock I tried to remind Hon. Members and Canadians generally what was in Canada's Constitution Act, 1982, a very recent document which indicated: "The existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed". "Recognition" means that Parliament and legislatures must recognize what aboriginal rights are, whether they be aboriginal rights to land, to fish, to hunt, to trap, or to carry on cultural activities.
We have had a miserable track record for more than a century in banning the Potlatch, a traditional Parliament which I am honoured to attend often in my own constituency where enormously important legal and constitutional matters take place. "Affirmation" means that the comprehensive claims process, the specific claims process, must be accelerated
Supply
to meet the constitutional objectives put before the people of Canada a short six years ago.
If one looks at some of the other cuts, one gets an idea of where the Government is going on what has been described by many, if not most, of the aboriginal leaders in Canada as a path leading to cultural genocide. Loans on comprehensive claims have been cut by over 20 per cent or by $10 million. One finds that in the Estimates under Section 2-36. Human resource development has been cut by over 50 per cent since 1986, according to Section 2-42 of the Estimates which were just tabled. There has been a cut of $24 million and a staff cut of 60 per cent. If we are not to be involved in the development of human resources, where is the Government intending to go? Renewable resource development was cut from $30 million in 1986 to $4 million. This is a cut of $26 million, as well as a cut from a staff of 28 to a staff of 4.
As I said earlier this morning, the only realizable increase in the budget of the Minister responsible for aboriginal affairs is a result of the intervention of the United Nations on the Lovelace case. We find paltry sums attached to new housing, post-secondary education, and some additional medical costs.
Let us take a look at some of the other cuts-a cut to selfgovernment from $13 million to $11 million; on comprehensive claims, from $78 million to $73 million; on economic development, from $82 million to $66 million; and on lands, reserves, and trusts, from $48 million to $41 million. In all key areas of development we find the Government cutting back enormously on the amount of funds available.
Let us take a look at the example of one part of a department, litigation funding and support for environmental protection, lands, funds, estates, and so on. We find that of the $41 million allocated-and I am quoting from the Minister's own Estimates-51.3 per cent relates to personnel costs. Over half is eaten up by the department itself. Some 22.9 per cent relates to other operating costs, so it is eaten up by the Department or by consultants to the department. Therefore, only 25.8 per cent is actually transferred on environmental protection, litigation support, specific claims, membership in band Governments, lands, funds, and estates. We find that only a quarter of the funds actually voted by Parliament reaches aboriginal peoples in their home communities.
I ask Hon. Members to reflect upon the following. While we found that the federal Budget has effectively tripled in the past decade, funding to aboriginal affairs in 1981 fixed dollars has remained effectively frozen. I asked the Parliamentary Library to go through all the documents-the Estimates, the actual expenditures, Treasury Board documents, and so on. Therefore, I realize that the funding to aboriginal people has effectively remained flat for a decade, whereas in almost all other areas of government expenditure it has doubled, tripled, or better.
We are finding aboriginal people frozen out of the constitutional process, frozen out of resource development impact funding, frozen out of litigation funding unless it is at the

March 17, 1988
Supply
appeal level, frozen out of funding for housing, and frozen out of economic development. It is a very sad state. I do not think any Canadian who has taken a close look at the reality of what is happening to aboriginal Canadians could in any way support a Government which continues to pursue that.
Over the past few months I had an opportunity to attend a meeting with Miles Richardson, President of the Council of the Haida Nation along with the Minister responsible for Indian Affairs. After an hour Miles Richardson finally put perhaps the most poignant question that has ever been put to the Minister in his political career. He asked him point blank: "What is your responsibility as the Minister of Indian Affairs to the Haida people?" The Minister responsible for aboriginal affairs, with me present, said nothing. He did not speak, indicating that his responsibility to aboriginal people such as those of the Haida Nation was nothing. It does not exist, yet he has a $2 billion budget, a huge Department over which he governs, and he rides around in a limousine.
The Nisga are here. Frank Calder is here. He has attempted to meet with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) and with the Minister responsible for aboriginal affairs for more than a year by letter, by telephone, and by telex. They have arrived here and have spent five days waiting for even five minutes to meet with either Minister. They were categorically refused meetings with the two Ministers who have the most direct responsibility to them.
In the area in which I live I represent the Haida, the Nisga, the Tsimshian, the Haisla, the Gitksan-Wet'suwet'en, the Tahltan, and the Tlingits, probably the most dense and most significant aboriginal populations south of the 60th parallel, amounting to well in excess of 25,000 aboriginal people in northwestern British Columbia.
I should like to spend a moment referring to the motion before the House. It condemns the Government for its failure to address the needs of the aboriginal people of Canada on self-government, shelter, health care, educational facilities, and so on. One need only look at the remarks of the Minister of Indian Affairs a couple of weeks ago in the House when I put a question to the Prime Minister about comprehensive claims. I asked where the Government was going and why the Prime Minister had never taken the opportunity to come to British Columbia and say: "Yes, it is the constitutional and legal responsibility of the Government of Canada to negotiate treaty settlements in British Columbia". There is only Treaty 8 and the Governor Douglas treaties of which there are 14. The rest of British Columbia must be involved in comprehensive negotiations with the first citizens of the area.
We have records in my own area in northwestern British Columbia on the Skeena, written records going back 10,000 years regarding trade on the Skeena, the Nass, and other systems in that area. Too many Canadians are unaware of the enormous, refreshing, and beautiful cultural and individual histories of the aboriginal people of this continent.
We can look internationally and find Convention 107 of the International Labour Organization. The Government, under the direction of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux), and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is arguing for assimilation of aboriginal people rather than standing up for them as persons and individual identifiable indigenous groups within Canada. It prefers to talk about them as minority populations in Canada. Fighting against that is the largest coalition of aboriginal groups in Canadian history, the Indigenous Working Group, which has fought long and hard.
More recently, before the United Nations subcommittee on human rights we found the Secretary of State for External Affairs and his officials in Geneva arguing against a study to look into treaties in Canada and for other indigenous populations around the world, well known, well identified, as the people on this planet the most at risk. Why would Canada be on the forefront of fighting against a study of treaties? One need only look at Mr. Nielsen's Buffalo Jump of the 1980s, the budget cuts, the refusal to move on comprehensive and specific claims, to see why. On specific claims, Mr. Speaker, 32 have been dealt with so far out of 428. We see specific claims funding cut from $30 million to $1 million between 1986 and this year. No government Member can travel around this country and tell any aboriginal person that there will be movement under Brian Mulroney-

-on comprehensive or specific claims if one looks at the funds voted before this House.
Let us look at another example in which the Minister has been involved in Alberta with the Lubicon. The committee, composed of a majority of government Members, voted to have E. Davie Fulton brought before the committee, voted to have E. Davie Fulton attached to the Lubicon negotiations as a mediator. The Minister categorically refused even though it was a majority vote that reported to this House. The Minister has refused to take the views of all Members of this House into consideration in appointing who, I might add, was John Diefenbaker's Minister of Justice, a renowned and respected Supreme Court Justice of British Columbia who was appointed by the same Government to look into the Lubicon situation. Instead, what does the Minister do? He provides $9.5 million to the Daishowa Paper Corporation, and the Alberta Government gives over 11,000 square miles of Alberta untendered, without an initial environmental evaluation, contrary to the Cabinet's own order. The Cabinet required an initial environmental evaluation for a pulp mill that will be immediately outside of the Wood Buffalo National Park. This is a pulp mill that will affect federal lands, not only a national park, and that will affect the aboriginal people who live within Wood Buffalo National Park, to say nothing of the impact that it has had on the Lubicon people.
March 17, 1988

I could go on at even greater length but I think the figures and the facts that I have placed on the record today sustain the argument that this Government is hell-bent on the cultural genocide of the aboriginal Inuit and Metis people of Canada, and it should be ashamed of it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to engage in this debate, especially in following the lead of our colleague, the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger), and his contribution to the debate. He has distinguished himself over the years that he has been here with his knowledge of Indian affairs and the future of Canada's native people. It is a special pleasure to be following him in this debate.
My purpose this afternoon is to set the record straight on the question of the health of Canada's original people and to bring Members up to date on the services which the federal Government provides through the medical services branch in my Department, a purpose which is to improve and maintain the health of Inuit and Indian people.
May I say at the outset that the Indian and northern health services work closely with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and that consultation with Indian leaders and Indian communities on issues affecting their health and health services is fundamental to the process of program development and implementation. I want to remind the House that in 1979, the Conservative Government restructured the federal Indian health policy. That short period of time we were in office resulted in that work.
This document, which was drafted by the now Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) for this Government, cast aside what we thought at that time were the restrictive and penny-pinching policies which the former Liberal Government has pursued. The Indian health policy recognizes for the first time the traditional relationship of the native people to the federal Government. Anyone who has studied constitutional law and that relationship comes naturally and inexorably to that conclusion. It also recognizes that there is but one system of health care in Canada consisting of federal, provincial and community or local elements as well as acknowledging that the health services provided for a native people are inseparable from the development of the community. In discussions with the AFN as recently as the last seven to ten days ago, that point has been made very clear again. I have been pleased to see how those discussions have been taking place and how a transfer of health policy is very much being seen as a model by the leadership with respect to a further move toward taking control of their lives and self-government.
The Indian health policy establishes the absolute need for increased active participation of Indian and Inuit communities in issues and programs affecting their health and well-being.
As a sign of good faith, in 1979 the Conservative Government withdrew the restrictive 1978 guidelines which had governed the provision of non-insured health benefits and
Supply
made medical transportation, prescription drugs, glasses, dental care and other items not covered by our national health insurance program available to all Indians and Inuits who required them. I find it, and I know this is not usually done in this House, passing strange that the Auditor General would have remarked in one of his reports that the expansion of those programs should be examined, namely, that expenditures are higher than normal expenditure increases in other departments. The reason was a large gap having to be filled, and that is what has been taking place. Perhaps the most important aspect of this policy is the Government's recognition of the special health needs of the native people. It is this recognition that has provided this Government with the incentive to increase funds for Indian and northern health services and to strengthen the programs needed to ensure that the health of our native people does not suffer unduly.
What about the health of the Inuit and Indian people? In the few moments I have I would like to quote statistics on the status of their health but before so doing, let me give you, Mr. Speaker, a few facts taken from Statistics Canada publication entitled Canada's Native People, published in 1979. I think it demonstrates how the Indian people suffered from years of Liberal neglect.
For example, at that time, when changes were made on those policies, over half of the status Indian population living on reserve had never gone to high school. Only about 42 per cent of Indian men and 22 per cent of Indian women living on reserve were employed. Almost one-quarter of on-reserve houses were in need of repair. Over 50 per cent did not have central heat, 32 per cent were overcrowded and 30 per cent lacked bathroom facilities.
All of us who represent native people and see what is happening on the reserves know that we still have a long distance to go, but I am pleased, at least in the 15 years I have been here, to see the changes that have taken place on some of those reserves. Local leadership has been taking control and by the use of government and private programs to my mind have made the progress that we see to date. We should commend those advances to other members of Canadian society rather than commending the stereotype we see so often which then colours, in my mind, a picture which is not true to the reality taking place. Data for the Inuit, I would think, would tell a similar story, so for lack of time I will not go into that at this stage.
The Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin has already advised this place of the steps that are being taken by the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs to improve conditions on reserves, improvements, may I say, that are long overdue. It is, however, this legacy which my Department must strive to provide or arrange for the provision of health to almost 600 Inuit reserves located in the 10 provinces and two territories as well as more than 50 Inuit communities across the land.
Let us look as a House what the status of health is of our native people. There are positive indications that health status

March 17, 1988
Supply
is improving, but the Indian and Inuit people still-I have said this in the document Achieving Health for All-have a long way to catch up to the level of health enjoyed by the majority of Canadians. We could also relate this to economic status. I think Members who represent native people also understand that.
In the more than 40 years which the medical services branch of the Department has provided health services to the native people there has been a marked decline in the rate of many infectious diseases, improvement in maternal, infant and child mortality rates. Remote and isolated communities have better access to hospital and medical services and to arrange preventive health programs. 1 think as well it should be stated that many people who have served in those communities, often very isolated, have been performing services as members of those communities in a manner which all of us should commend. From time to time we forget about that. When I visit the health stations, especially seeing the nurses in those stations and the community health representatives, the CHRs, I am always impressed with their dedication. It should also be said to Members of the House that some CHRs and native people have had service to their community and the department extending well beyond 10 and 15 years. That service has been given at the local level as well.
However, to my mind, the health status of Inuit and Indians still remains unacceptably low when compared with that of other Canadians. For example, from 1982 to 1985 the post neo-natal mortality rate of Canadian Indians was 10.9 per cent per 1,000 live births. That compares very unfavourably with a rate of only three per thousand for non-Indian infants. Life expectancy for Indian males is 62.4 years compared to 71.9 years for the Canadian male population as a whole. Indian women have a life expectancy of 68.9 years compared to 78.9 years for the Canadian female population as a whole.
The leading causes of Inuit and Indian death are accidents, violence and poisonings. Deaths from injuries and poisonings are at least three times higher than the corresponding rate for the general Canadian population. Infant mortality, and I think all of us would be pleased at this, has declined, but from a rate of 39.6 per 1,000 live births in 1974 to about 17 per thousand today. While this is commendable, I would point out that the infant mortality rate for Indians and Inuit is still almost twice the national rate and, therefore, unacceptable.
Suicide in all circumstances is tragic, but for the Indian people of Canada it is catastrophic. In the 15 to 19 age group, the rate is almost seven and a half times higher than national rates for young people. Between the ages of 20 and 24 the rate is almost five and a half times higher. For the Inuit in 1985, of a total of 224 deaths from all causes, nine were suicides. They were all people under the age of 34. The causes of suicide are broken homes, lack of employment opportunities, alienation, and inability to achieve expectations. While never fully addressed, I believe people in the community, Canadians who
are serving in various departments, are trying to address these most complex and difficult issues. However, it will take time to undo the years of suffering and neglect which have characterized the way of life of Canada's aboriginal people.
These major health problems are related to social and environmental conditions. Improvement in health status cannot be achieved by medical technology alone. In fact, sometimes the easiest thing to deliver is medical technology. However, it is the social, psychological and economic foundations that are so difficult to change. More emphasis must be placed on health promotion and disease prevention strategies which respond to the social, economic and environmental realities of Indian communities and which give those communities control over the planning and delivery of relevant health programs.
I think I have been very forthright in stating the issues. I have not tried to colour them in any way. However, the Government does recognize the disparities that exist between the health and well-being of the Inuit and Indian people with that of Canadians as a whole. I would like to take just a few minutes to inform my colleagues in this place of a few of the initiatives under way to ameliorate conditions and reduce these disparities.
The 1988-89 Estimates recently tabled in this House include almost $46 million for the National Native Alcohol and Drug Abuse Program, or NNADAP. It supports Indian and Inuit community alcohol and drug prevention programs, including community awareness, alcohol and drug abuse counselling services, in-patient and out-patient facilities for detoxification, and rehabilitation. That includes monitoring and continuing treatment. Of course, NNADAP provides training for counsellors and others working in the field of alcohol and drug abuse.
I have a NNADAP facility on one of the reserves in my riding. I asked an elder in that community why are there so few people from the reserve attending the program. It is not that the program is not full, but it is not full of members of that community. I thought he put it in a very practical way, and we have a lesson to learn here. So often we like to bring in programs for Indian and Inuit people which are different from the norm in the rest of Canada. He said if you built an alcohol and drug rehabilitation centre on the main street of any one of your towns, would the local townspeople come to the front door for treatment? I think he pointed out in a very practical and succinct way the kinds of problems we face. I opened a NNADAP centre not long ago in Qu'Appelle, Saskatchewan. They are trying to unite the very best techniques we know of in alcohol and drug abuse rehabilitation with native workers and the spiritual history of native people.
The NNADAP program has been working well, but I am concerned that some of the beds, for example, cost almost as much as hospital care and we are not getting enough rehabilitation. However, those are the administrative realities of these programs and something we have to be vigilant about. We have to bring it back to the goal of rehabilitation rather than
March 17, 1988

looking at it, as some like to do, as economic development for a given region.
I spoke earlier of the Government's commitment to consultation with the native people. I should also bring to your attention some of the steps being taken to involve Indians and Inuit more thoroughly in the control and provision of their own health care. A modest but important program is the Indian-Inuit Professional Health Careers Development Program. This is part of a more comprehensive strategy designed to coordinate the education and training in health needs of the native people so that they can acquire the education and skills to become health providers to their own people. Over $2 million and 28 person-years have been allocated to that important thrust.
Through the Non-insured Health Benefits Program, qualified native people now receive prescription drugs, we think good dental care, and eyeglasses to correct visual defects. Transportation to medical care is also an important feature of the program and many Indian bands and Inuit settlements now run their own transportation programs to take their people to hospitals or medical clinics. Just to show you the scope of the program, in 1987-88 over $200 million was spent on these benefits. Native people living in isolation in northern parts of the provinces or territories are evacuated by air to hospitals in the larger cities or in the south. There is no question of their being denied access to the best of health services and care that Canada can provide.
I know there is criticism from time to time that the evacuation should not take place and we should have more health facilities in the regions. We are building a hospital at Yellowknife right now, for example. I see the Hon. Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin) here and she will probably want to talk about the Whitehorse General as well. Those are the kinds of initiatives taking place. However, we always have to keep distances and isolation in mind when we try to address some of these questions.
Where, in earlier days, mothers had their babies at home or at nursing stations, today over 95 per cent of native births occur in hospital. Maternity mortality has been virtually eliminated. Mortality in the one to four age group continues to decline and I am confident the rate will be no greater than the national rate within a short period of time. However, as you may have learned from my remarks, the health of Canada's aboriginal people is a major concern of the Government. We are attempting, with the co-operation and participation of native people and their leaders, to implement new initiatives for Indian and Inuit health. One area of the utmost priority to my department is the transfer of health services to Indian management and control. For example, responsibility for the delivery of health services in the Northwest Territories will be transferred from Health and Welfare to the territorial Government in April of this year.

In North Battleford, The Battlefords Indian Health Centre runs the Indian Health Program for reserves in that district. Finally, we recently transferred the Baffin from the department to a local hospital board representing the entire region of the Baffin. We put forward a proposal to the people of the Baffin, centred in Iqaluit to demonstrate that this could work. I cannot put it in any better bureaucratise than that. It was my argument that it would work. As a former member of a local hospital board, I have always been a great believer that you deliver services best at the local level.
It did work, Mr. Speaker. People in the area were deeply concerned about their health care system. We have transferred the Baffin and are now going to transfer the entire Northwest Territories. In 1979 I thought that the Yukon would be first, but the NWT will be first. We are also negotiating south of sixty.
Why is health important? I am sure that my colleague who reports to this House for the Post Office might not like this, but all polling indicates that of all the services which Canadians receive from various levels of government health care rates nearest the top in every survey, even higher than services regarding the Post Office.
However, in all seriousness, in the 15 years that I have dealt with health care as a former Minister of Indian Affairs and now as Minister of Health, there has been tremendous progress made. We have some distance to go yet, and I fully recognize that, keeping in mind the isolation of Indian and Inuit communities.
However, let us celebrate the things that are working well. Let us work at changing those things about which none of us are happy. I still have not addressed, for instance, the matter of health with regard to status people off the reserve. That is an entire area for which I have not time today.
I believe sincerely that the progress which we have seen has been largely due to two things; one, local community leaders taking control of the health situation in their communities, cajoling government and others to move forward on agendas which they have put forward for so many years and, second,

dedicated workers. I will stand on any platform and commend the people whom I have seen in these communities delivering health care, native people and non-native people. If the system is working, it is largely due to them.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the time you have given me in the House to put some of these matters on the record.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments and a question or two for the Minister. I would like to start by thanking him for joining the debate which I, on behalf of our caucus started earlier today. I agree with him in some of his concluding remarks. I believe that local leadership has made a vast difference in the last 10 to 15 years. I also believe that the facilities offered by the federal Government indicate a vast improvement over the last 10 to 15 years. I will credit both of the two previous Governments for that. I also agree with the Minister that there is a long way to go.
However, one area in which there has been a constant, chronic shortage is in the supply of nurses to the remote areas. The Minister himself has spoken about that in the past. The concern that I have raised in this House with the Government and previous Governments is that we never have a large enough pool of nurses available. That means that when there are one or two nurses in St. Theresa, or other parts of the Provencher riding which will soon be part of the Churchill riding, they are overworked. The stress and various other problems result in a high turnover. Many of those people are very dedicated and would love to stay in the North for a longer time. I spoke only a month ago with the last nurse who left. She just could not handle it anymore. She was not getting relief. She was not allowed to go out when she was scheduled to go out. She was on call on an almost continuous basis.
I hope that in replying to me the Minister will indicate that there will be some increase in the pool of nurses in order that the situation of the last eight years, in which there is always a shortage of nurses in northern Manitoba, and I am sure elsewhere across the country, will not continue.
I also hope that in the Minister's reply he will deal with the need for nursing homes. A number of the larger reserves would like to have nursing homes. There are no facilities for seniors in the communities. Oxford House is one community which is concerned about this. This is especially important because there are not proper water, sewage, and other facilities in these communities for individuals 75 or 80 years old. To live in houses heated by wood which have no other facilities is very difficult. I am also concerned about developing a better home care program for people who would like to stay in the communities.
As a final point, I believe that there should be some minimal legislation with regard to water and sewage in these communities. Any other municipality would fall under provincial or some other regulation and I believe it is necessary to have, not only guidelines but a legal requirement for the federal Government to maintain minimum standards.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that Members of the House will be surprised that I agree with many of the things which the Hon. Member has raised. We have worked on some of them together. With regard to nurses, the Hon. Member is correct about the shortages. There is a turnover in all places but there does not seem to be as much turnover in the Northwest Territories as there is on some of the reserves south of sixty which, in some ways, are more difficult to get in and out of than are areas further north. That does not apply in all cases but does apply in some.
I was given a very good reception in Thompson not long ago. I talked to my staff there about the nursing shortage, the turnover, and relief help. I would like to build up a pool as well. We are advertising for nurses, not only in the Canadian context but abroad as well. Some people argue that that is not the best way, that we should be training more native nurses. I agree with that but, on the other hand, many areas have been served very faithfully by people who came to Canada, went into some of the remote communities, and became very valued members of those communities. Therefore, it is a balancing. I would indeed like to have a pool of nurses, as suggested by the Hon. Member, in order that we can administer the provision of services better than we are at the present time.
With regard to nursing homes, extended care, and home care, I mentioned in my speech that there are gaps and that we have some distance to go in order to catch up with the rest of Canadian society. We have done some of that work. Through CMHC we now have some housing for seniors on reserves. It is still a matter of how much personal care we can provide. The argument is that the elders of a community must leave their community and live their last years outside of the community of which they have been members all their lives.

March 17, 1988

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for the question. I am sure he had it cleared through the Liberal caucus first, and that there is full agreement from the Liberal Party on the proposition he makes. But I do not want to be facetious in an area like this.
