subsubtopic: ALLOTED DAY, S. O. 82-RIGHTS OF ABORIGINAL PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to deal with the opposition motion moved by the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) condemning the Government for its failure to address the needs of the aboriginal people of Canada. The subject which interests me most is item b) dealing with shelter and health care.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend my colleague the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) for his tireless interest in the Indian Affair issue, the excellent speech he made in the House this morning, and especially for his dedication to the Liberal Party caucus. As a result of his efforts and interest, the future of our native poeple seems a little brighter.
In his wisdom, the United Nations General Assembly proclaimed 1987 as the International Year of the Homeless and an important conference was held here in Ottawa, from September 13 to 16 of that year. During this conference, we learned that in 1987, 100,000 people were homeless in Canada, many of them are natives and the majority come down to the cities of Winnipeg and Vancouver.

March 17, 1988
Supply
In 1988 the homeless are different from those of the 1930s. Their faces have changed. These are no longer older men. These are no longer tramps. These are young people, some of them women, and we can see entire families sleeping in parks, tents or trucks.
Last year, in 1987, the average age of homeless men and women was 34 and 33, respectively. Six months after the international conference the Government has yet to make arrangements to solve the problem. The consequences are serious, particularly among native people where cases of tubeculosis are increasing alarmingly, even among children. Most native people live in small overcrowded accommodations-sometimes four, five to a room-in unhealthy and cold tenements.
So what are the results, Mr. Speaker? The results are problems of mental health, alcoholism or drug abuse which, as we all know, lead to emotional, physical or sexual abuse. Young Indians living in such conditions become school dropouts, they grow careless and irresponsible, and they are a burden to society.
I recall that when I sat on the special committee on the handicapped we went up north to listen to testimony, and all chairs in the front rows were occupied by young people, most of them between the ages of 15 and 20. My curiosity was aroused and I asked for an explanation. The native spokesman explained that these young people took their skidoos, their radio-cassette players and large quantities of alcohol, and organized parties. As they were too drunk to drive their skidoos safely back, they often had accidents. What is even worse, is that, while the dog teams always brought them back home, skidoos are prone to mechanical problems and the young people do not have the knowledge or the means to repair them. They sometimes wake up the next morning with frozen hands and feet. Whose fault is it? I believe that the Canadian Government has a very large part of the responsibility in that.
The first solution would be to ensure that Canadian native people have decent and adequate housing. What does decent housing mean? To help Hon. Members understand better what I mean, I shall describe the house of a native family which I saw with my own eyes in Goose Bay, Labrador. The streets were winding and in bad repair. Garbage was stored on scaffolding to prevent the animals from getting at it. Shingles were missing from the roof. There was electricity, but no running water. There was a bed in the kitchen, which shows how cramped the living quarters were.
I was a member of the Committee on the Handicapped, and after this visit, we were driven over a bridge. We found ourselves in another world. The streets were clean and well maintained. There was no garbage and the whole atmosphere spoke of success. This is where the white people lived. Just imagine the child who comes back from school to a house like the one I have just described in Goose Bay, Labrador. This
child has no chance in life. His whole environment is negative, without mentioning the emotional problems related to such an environment.
Mr. Speaker, to break out of this never-ending vicious circle we have to begin at square one, and that is to make sure that all our native people have a solid and decent roof over their heads. But what are the conditions? There are conditions, if we are to solve the problem. As housing critic for the Official Opposition I learned that 80 per cent of all housing units on Indian reserves have been built since 1961. Given the fact that Indian homes are not expected to last much more than 16 to 20 years, no wonder many of them have become woefully inadequate and in need of major repairs. Be that as it may, independent government surveys have shown that 73 per cent of all housing units on Indian reserves are inadequate. In addition, these units are rapidly deteriorating because of overcrowding: 7.5 per cent of all native single-family housing units are home to more than one family, whereas the corresponding figure for non-native families is 1.4 per cent.
It has been estimated that only 3 per cent of non-natives exceed the average of one person per room, while the comparable figure for Indian on reserves is 35 per cent, which means that slightly more than one third are over that average. The incidence of overcrowding is particularly acute among Western Canadian natives. To put it in a nutshell, I would say that native housing units are 21 times more likely to be overcrowded than non-native units.

Statistics from a study conducted during the International Year of the Shelter for the Homeless demonstrates further the poor living conditions in Indian housing. The proportion of dwellings on reserves requiring major repairs is 23 per cent, with 37 per cent having inadequate bathroom facilities and 37 per cent having no bathroom at all. The number of dwellings lacking central heating is estimated to be more than 50 per cent of all reserve dwellings.
About 34 per cent of Indian dwellings lack a piped waste disposal system or septic tank and 18 per cent have no kitchen sink. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, living in a house with no kitchen sink? If we were talking about non-Indian housing, we would be describing a slum.
We must also take into consideration the fact that the average personal income for Indians is only 50 per cent of the non-Indian population. Personal income among the young and elderly is below the Statistics Canada poverty line. One can imagine the situation for Indians with no income at all. Eighty-three per cent of the Indian population have an annual income [DOT]which is less than $10,000 per year. Only 4 per cent of the Indian population earn more than $20,000.
I am especially saddened by the effect of this situation on Indians. The average death rate for Indians from infections and parasite diseases is higher per 100,000 than the Canadian
March 17, 1988

average. Bad sanitary installations, when there are any, are partly responsible for this situation.
Bill C-31 adds to the overcrowding on reserves. Although this Bill is very positive and necessary, it has its drawbacks. More people are returning to the reserves, and funds needed to meet this influx are not sufficient. This adds to the already existing backlog in housing units. Ninety-five thousand people have filed claims to return to the reserves of Canada and most of these claims have come from women. Further, Indian women and their children who are trying to return to the reserves are having a lot of problems. They cannot have access to housing on reserves until the existing backlog of houses has been dealt with. Once again, the women of Canada are paying the price. Indians are among the very worst served and most needy of all Canadians.
At a recent meeting of the Committee on Government Operations dealing with Native housing, officials from the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs told us that funds earmarked for Native housing have not increased in four years. Indeed, taking inflation into account, there has been a reduction in the amounts allocated for the construction of houses on Indian reserves.
Natives who appeared before the Committee have confirmed their extremely serious situation. Management criteria for those programs and obligations imposed on Indian bands are too complex.
I should point out to Honourable Members of this House the nightmare lived by the Fairford Indian band. Beside all the money problems with various government authorities, they experienced right from the start humidity condensation problems in their "new" houses.
The chief of the Fairford band told us that the clothes of the children and grown-ups living in these houses smelled damp and that the smell was pervasive inside their homes, rain or shine.
This morning I heard the first Conservative speaker say that the aboriginal people were going ahead without waiting for the Government to act. What the Hon. Member fails to understand is that we have erected barriers that prevent aboriginal people from becoming full-fledged citizens. The most striking example as far as housing is concerned, is the fact that aboriginal people on the reserve do not have access to mortgages. This means they cannot own their own homes. The Crown owns the land on which their homes are built. This causes problems, not just for the aboriginal people but also for construction contractors, because if there are any money problems as a result of bureaucratic red-tape, they often do not get paid because the band does not have enough money or for any number of bureaucratic reasons.
Supply
I agree that the circumstances of aboriginal people have improved, but not enough to make them entirely satisfactory. I pointed out earlier that the aboriginal people are the neediest in our society, and much remains to be done before I could consider their situation a thing of the past.
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of success stories, but these are the typical result of political will on the part of aboriginal and non-aboriginal governments.
In Quebec, for instance, we have examples of aboriginal companies such as Air Creebec, Cree Yamaha, the Wemindji hydro-electric dam, Cree Construction, the New-Quebec cooperatives, Air Inuit, and of course various businesses set up by the Mohawks of Kahnawake and the Hurons of Lorette-ville. Similar examples may be found in other parts of the country. However, this does not mean all problems have been solved. These groups still have to put up with conditional subsidies and with the complexities and delay caused by bureaucratic tape, and so forth.
The experiment initiated by the CEGEP in Sept-Iles which set up a curriculum adapted to the needs of Native people is unique. But how many of these programs do we have in this country? Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, there are far too many obstacles to be overcome before any more projects like the ones I just mentioned can be considered.
What seems to be lacking is the political will. There is also not enough co-operation between Ministers and the various departments involved in seeking solutions. I asked the parliamentary committee how many times a year the Ministers and senior officials of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, National Health and Welfare, CMHC, Employment and Immigration and Treasury Board actually met? There are problems with all these departments, which keep passing the buck, and meanwhile, the aboriginal people have to wait.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding I want to say that I hope the Government will have the political will to take action very shortly.

subsubtopic: ALLOTED DAY, S. O. 82-RIGHTS OF ABORIGINAL PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure and, indeed, an honour to take part in this debate today on the question of addressing the needs of native people in Canada. I speak as a Member of Parliament for a north and western Saskatchewan constituency which has 19 Indian reserves and many other so-called non-status Indian communities. The most recent census shows that over one in five of my constituents are identified as being of native ancestry.
The issue of native rights, native housing, economic development and the right of native people to pursue determination for themselves are some of the most compelling issues that face many western Canadian communities today. It is therefore a real pleasure for me to take part in this discussion this afternoon in the House of Commons and to address a few

March 17, 1988
Supply
thoughts on the motion that has been put on this very important question of the status of the Indian person in Canada today.
I begin by cautioning not only the opposition critics who have spoken, but many of the viewers of this debate either in the gallery or at home through television, that we should examine the place of the native person in Canada today by way of a general overview. Every one of us who lives in a native community recognizes all too clearly the difficult plight facing Canada's native people. They have higher than the national average infant mortality rates, lower life expectancy than non-native Canadians and problems with alcohol, drugs and substance abuse that are indeed endemic in many native populations. These are all too clearly chronicled.
I wish to attempt in this debate to take a more constructive bent on the discussion by asking the following questions. Where are we moving? From where have we come in the past few years?
The problems facing many native communities have been present, at least in my area of the country, since the very day that many of the treaties were signed. In our area many of those treaties were signed in the period between 1875 and 1878. Thus we are not dealing with simply the modern urban contemporary problems, we are dealing with the problems of often dispossessed people that have vexed Canadian Governments for the past 110 years.
I have the sense that like all communities, the native population of Canada is in many respects in a time of transition. There are now native communities that are indeed far ahead of the planners, the developers and the bureaucrats and those in the Department of Indian Affairs and those so-called experts on native issues who examine the way that they would like to see native communities develop. Indeed, there are some of these communities that are as advanced in our area of Saskatchewan as many non-native communities. However, unfortunately, there are a greater number of communities that are still struggling with many of the basic questions of community organization.
I wish to say that it is not all as gloomy, as dark and as hopeless as certain people throughout the debate today have described the whole question of native life in Canada as being. In fact, I often invite critics from other Parties who perhaps do not live and work in native communities to come to a large area of western Canada in Saskatchewan, Alberta, or Manitoba to see those communities that are the success stories. We know as well that there are many communities which are indeed sad failures to date.
As fundamental to the development of a people as any desire or goal is the question of pursuing the ability, the right and determination to govern oneself. I wish to address my remarks this afternoon to the subject of native self-government. It is all too infrequent that we have the opportunity as Members of Parliament to address this important issue. I take considerable consolation that all three Parties in the House of Commons
have agreed with the basic direction being taken by the Government on the policy of Indian self-government.
It was in 1983 that an all-Party committee of the House of Commons, well chaired by the Hon. Member for Cochrane- Superior (Mr. Penner), the Liberal Member of Parliament who spoke earlier today, highlighted self-government as an appropriate goal and a valid response to the political aspirations of the Indian people. Self-government was recognized as the element of a unique relationship between Indian people and the Government of Canada, a relationship that would enable Indian people to take charge of the decisions that affect their lives. It would also help break the cycle of dependency that has for too long characterized the relationship between Indian communities and the federal Government.
It has only been in the past 20 years that Governments have begun to abandon the old paternalistic policy which was used when they dealt with native people. It was during the 1970s that the Government's initial response was to transfer the administration of various programs and services directly to Indian bands. Unfortunately, there have been some unsuccessful efforts to enact comprehensive or framework legislation that would be related to self-government.
I should note that significant promising developments in structural change did not begin to happen until only three years ago when this Government established as a priority the changing way in which we should deal with the relationship between native people and the federal Government. Early on in the mandate it became very clear to our Government that the top down, single, monolithic approach does not work. Aboriginal communities are far too diversified to be squeezed into one model of self-government. Since the start of our mandate in 1984 we have taken significant measures to support the development of initiatives for self-government. Our policies recognize the vital role that Canada's aboriginal communities play in the development of this Canada. Our actions express our commitment to further developing a relationship with Indian people which is built on mutual trust and confidence.
I would like Hon. Members to consider for a moment the different routes that the Government has taken to support the development of self-government for Indian people. The federal Government remains committed to the objective of selfgovernment for aboriginal people entrenched in the Constitution of Canada. This is the surest way that we can achieve permanent and fundamental change in the relationship between Indian people and the federal Government.
The federal proposal which was presented to the First Ministers in March, 1987 is still on the table. This amendment would recognize an explicit right to self-government to be implemented through a series of negotiated agreements. There has not been an agreement on this amendment, but as a Government we are not deterred by the failure of consensus. We are still open to the possibility of renewed constitutional
March 17, 1988

talks when the chances of an agreement look reasonably promising. In the meantime, we are determined to support the development of self-government to the greatest extent possible within the existing constitutional framework.
This Government has established a process for negotiating self-government agreements with Indian communities which provide the chance for those communities to move beyond the present limits of the Indian Act. The response to this policy has been very encouraging. We have received 60 proposals from more than 225 Indian bands, and are actively working on approximately 40 proposals at the present time. These proposals represent a wide geographical, historical, social, and cultural set of economic circumstances. In addition, the Government has implemented some new financial relationships with a number of Indian bands under self-government legislation and under what are known as alternative funding arrangements.
At this point, I wish to relate a story that is moving and encouraging. It involves one tribal council in the area in which I live in Saskatchewan. It involves the Meadow Lake Tribal Council which is a group of 10 bands that work together in a tribal council area and are presently negotiating a selfgovernment agreement with the Government of Canada. The Meadow Lake Tribal Council is a testament to what ingenuity, conviction and hard work will do for Indian communities. Some of the reserves in the Meadow Lake Tribal Council have suffered great economic difficulties and are still struggling to find their sense of identity and development.
Conversely, there are several bands in this tribal council area that are indeed the anchors to making this system work. For some time this tribal council has entirely managed its own education system. It is now moving into full health care administration. The entire infrastructure of local government is under control of the tribal council. This group, under the direction of its executive director, Ray Ahenakew, and Chief Percy Derocher, Chief Richard Gladue, Chief Fred Martell, and other chiefs within this vast area of northern Saskatchewan, is showing what working in a unified way can do to bring full development to native communities. I am exceedingly proud of the Meadow Lake Tribal Council and what it has done to work with the Government in planning a self-government agreement. I am confident that in the coming months we will be able to effect some type of workable long term solution to the question of self-government. It is only a matter of time for this tribal council, because it is an organization that is working to develop a very promising future for economic and political self-government.
Across Canada the path to self-government and selfsufficiency is not without some tough challenges. I believe that those challenges can be met. The cycle of poverty and dependence faced by many native communities can be broken. The federal Government, and where appropriate the provincial Governments, must work together with native communities at the local level. For Indian communities it means dedicating the
Supply
energy, the ideas, and the initiatives to establish local institutions that reflect local circumstances. For Government, it means that our policies, legislation, and resources, should enable the Indian communities to develop the types of structures and economic base which satisfies the needs of the community, and we hope that ultimately it will fit in with the Canadian constitutional framework.
The self-government policy of this Government is guided by the following basic principles which I wish to enunciate at this point. The policy must substantially increase local control and decision-making capability. It must be flexible enough to recognize the diverse needs, culture, and tradition of Indian people. The policy must lead to greater accountability of Indian leadership to their own electors rather than to a federal bureaucracy.
The process that we are striving for and indeed succeeding with native communities must be community based and supported by native communities. Self-government must be conducted at a measured pace. It must have a practical focus. In all cases, it must be tailored to the specific circumstances of the Indian community involved. Thus far, our policy has responded to specific needs. It can take into account circumstances such as the geographic location of the community, the availability of services, and the strength of the resource base in the area.
For a moment, I wish to consider Bill C-93, the Sechelt Indian Band Self-Government Act which this Parliament passed into law last year. Hon. Members will know that this Act is an enabling piece of legislation which has established the Sechelt community in British Columbia as the legal entity with a power to borrow money and hold property. The community received fee simple title to its land and it is now able to manage those lands according to the band's constitution. In short, the Sechelt people now have a Government which is accountable to the electors of the area and not to a remote bureaucracy in Ottawa.
If there is one part of the Mulroney Government's community self-government policy in which I can take particular pride, it is the consultative nature of the process. I recall well our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) saying during the 1984 election a very simple statement: "First you listen, then you act". That is a truism to most of us. Unfortunately, all too often in the process of government that does not become evident. I am pleased that our Government in this selfgovernment policy believes that individual native Canadians know best and can define best what they need and indeed what they must have.
We did not sit down in Ottawa and draft our views on what natives should do next. We asked Indian people, and we did it by saying: "We are open to you. Come to us with your ideas of what you want to do". That is what we have done, that is what native people have done, and I submit, in a large part, it is now beginning to work.

I salute the Minister for his untiring efforts and his dedication to ensuring for the families and children of Canadian native communities a potential future which will see them into the mainstream of Canadian society with all the rights, privileges, and ability to raise their families secure in the knowledge that a bright future awaits them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTED DAY, S. O. 82-RIGHTS OF ABORIGINAL PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak today on the motion before us. It is certainly an extremely important matter in the Yukon and in other areas of the Northwest Territories and across Canada. It is an issue in which I have been very much involved for a number of years. I feel very strongly and passionately that it requires much more debate in the House of Commons.
We clearly have a sad history in terms of the treatment of our aboriginal people. Neither the Liberal Government nor the current Tory Government has addressed the issue in a way which fundamentally facilitates the self-sufficiency and independence of Canada's first nations. We have a responsibility as politicians to deal with the mistakes of the past and to plan for the future. I suggest that this issue of all issues in Canada stands out as a shameful failure on the part of Canadian politicians and Canadian people.
In my view, much of the problem stems from the fact that we have taken a very colonialist attitude in coming to Canada and taking over the lands of aboriginal people. Aboriginal people, as some Canadians may not remember, were not a conquered people. This is why there have been many treaties with our aboriginal people. We did not win a war with them. We came. Treaties were made, sometimes under rather dubious circumstances so that we could use their land.
The basis of many of today's discussions and of the discussion of the previous speaker on the issue of self-government- and I will expand on it later for a few minutes-is the principle of aboriginal rights. It is something that many Canadian citizens have some trouble understanding and, in some instances, accepting. I think it is important to begin this discussion by establishing that this is a right which has been accepted in Canada by all political Parties. It is an established right based on a claim of first priority, that aboriginal people were the first citizens here. They were not a conquered people. From that flow a number of rights to them which take the form of certain programs, perhaps the self government question and a number of other treaty rights.
The problem has been that no government, as I said earlier, has taken these rights seriously by honoring them in a way in which a government should. This is not, I suggest, a result of some malevolent plan. It is not a result of people being unfair or mean spirited. It is a result of fundamentally not understanding both the historical reality of aboriginal rights and the reality of a different culture. Certainly as the adage goes, whoever defines the problem defines the solution. We as nonaboriginal people have been defining solutions for far too many
Supply
years. We see by the programs that they are very inadequate solutions.
There are a number of examples of how historically we have begun to look at the question of aboriginal issues in Canada. First, when we as colonists came to this country-and historians I am sure will agree with this-we thought the Indian and the aboriginal people would simply die out. But they did not. In fact, despite disease and many other factors, they have continued to flourish in our society and have a very high birth rate.
Then there was the hope that the aboriginal people would assimilate into the greater society. Then there was the traumatic establishment of residential schools where children, without parental permission, were taken where they would learn English and learn to be useful citizens, as it was defined at that time. They were punished for speaking their own language. Most of their schools were closed only in the late 1960s, but we still see the extremely traumatic results of attempting to eradicate a culture. That policy did not work.
From 1969 up to the famous Chretien White Paper and the strong reaction of the aboriginal people to that, there began to be some funding of aboriginal organizations. They became much stronger and much more forceful advocates for their own distinct interests. Part of the policy that I referred to in changing views of aboriginal people, within the context of Canadian society, was how people could lose their status. It is hard for most tourists to imagine a situation where you could be one day an Indian and the next day, if you had gone to war to fight for this country or you had become a doctor, a lawyer or, if you were a woman and had married a non-Indian, you were not an Indian. Most of us would find that rather difficult to accept. Of course, it was patently unfair and we are now dealing with the results of that kind of policy.
Bill C-31 referred to by other speakers is an example of where we have tried to redress some of this discrimination by restoring status to Indian women and their children who married non-aboriginal people and lost their status. We have seen some of the problems emanating from that. Mopping up history, Mr. Speaker, is an expensive business. We have done it as a society with decided reluctance rather than with a sense of fairness and justice, as should have been the case in a democratic society.
I would like to give a few examples relating to the motion before us in the House today. Sections in the motion around the housing and education programs and so on are examples of the failure to take seriously the commitment of addressing historical realities. For instance, funding of aboriginal programs. If you look closely at the funding, you will see what we have done is predicate it on a welfare basis so that people, groups or organizations receive just enough to keep alive, but rarely enough on which to flourish and develop. I could give many, many examples.
There are very few programs that have permanent funding. Often it is annual funding, sometimes five year funding but

March 17, 1988
Supply
rarely permanent funding so that a plan can be made and security for staff for a fundamental change. This is the point about the lack of serious commitment to aboriginal issues. You ask about examples of the kinds of programs of which I am speaking, Mr. Speaker. There are the friendship centres, about 99 across Canada, which offer many programs and employment for aboriginal people. They have just finished a five year funding cycle. We do not know what is going to happen. They do not know what is going to happen, yet they provide a useful service.
Communication societies across this country include native newspapers, broadcasting and so on. Native newspapers have not received any increase in funding in the last six years in order to hire staff and get the ordinary cost of living that all of us, including all of us in this House, expect every year. What about funding to band councils and band governments? Then there is education and training. My colleague from Skeena talked earlier today about the decrease in funding for land claims, economic development, housing and the devolving of programs.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) this afternoon spoke about the devolution of programs to native peoples. I believe this Minister sincerely has tried very hard to work on that issue. However, sincerity is not enough. The money has to go with it. What has happened, if you look closely at the record, Mr. Speaker, is that what the Government and the previous Government did was say:, "Fine, we will let you run the program. We will give you the rule book. It will be our rules, not your rules. We will not give you any administration money but we will give you the program dollars and you can run it". That is characteristic of the way we have dealt with aboriginal people. We have said: "You play by our rules, do it our way or else we will not help you in your community".
I think the issue of land claims is where we must clearly see the philosophies and attitudes prevailing. In my view, particularly in my own riding of the Yukon where there have been ongoing land claim negotiations for 15 years which have not been resolved, for a two year period from about 1984 to 1986 the Government withdrew from negotiations and said that we had to come up with policy. So we are working on the policy. We now have a policy with extremely narrow guidelines and negotiations are under way again. Everyone has heard of the Lubicon situation where in order to get justice the Lubicon Indians had to take advantage of an international event, the Olympics, in Calgary. This surely is not the way to give justice to aboriginal people.
As I mentioned, in the Yukon with the ongoing negotiations, we are beginning to see that less funding is available for research by native bands into land claims negotiations. This is not just in the Yukon, but elsewhere, and they cannot be expected to do the kind of research necessary in order to take their negotiating positions in a meaningful way with decreased funding. That is happening over and over again.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) has not been actively involved in these negotiations. He has not taken the interest to see that they are settled. It is crucial that these claims be settled. It is detrimental to the aboriginal communities and to the non-aboriginal communities to see, as in the Yukon, land ownership tied up until we can settle what land quantum will be given to Indian peoples or will be negotiated by Indian peoples. I believe strongly, and we have some examples such as the Inuvialuit agreement, that with political will land claims can be settled. Negotiators need to have a mandate which means that they can negotiate at the local level, not run back to Ottawa every five minutes to get some agreement on it. A politician in the Yukon once said that much of governing in the North is like driving a team of horses with reins 3,000 miles long. It does not work and is not working in land claims, which is an extremely important example of a lack of commitment to seriously deal with aboriginal issues.
I would like to now talk about self-government to which the previous speaker referred. Self-government is an essential part of land claims. Land claims is not just about land, it is about economic development and control over one's life. The history of the treatment of aboriginal peoples has been one of someone else defining how things will be done. It has not worked.
It was interesting to hear the previous speaker talk about self-government and government policy. It was instructive to hear him outline how the Government had listened to aboriginal people and is interested in listening. I will tell you that probably no other people have been listened to as much as the aboriginal people. We have had numerous task forces, the Penner report on self-government, the Cooligan report, as well as many others with many recommendations which have never been implemented. Aboriginal people are probably the most over-listened-to people in Canada. They probably come next to the poor, I guess, with all the poverty studies. What has not happened is action resulting from all that listening.
The previous speaker referred to individual definitions of self-government and how the Government had listened to what aboriginal people had to say. Why have they not listened to aboriginal people who have said entrench self-government in the Constitution? That is what aboriginal people are asking for. We have First Ministers' Conferences that go on for four or five years and the issue cannot be resolved. Yet in one day or one night the First Ministers sit down and change the character of this country through the Meech Lake Accord.
What we have is not, as is often referred to, an Indian problem. We have a problem with non-aboriginal people who refuse to look at the situation in its cultural context. They refuse to give up a shred of power to Canada's first nations and implement the kind of fairness that should be a hallmark of this country.
March 17, 1988

In that same vein I would like to talk about the lack of recognition of the traditional life-styles of aboriginal people. Yes, we like moccasins and handicrafts and feel that is pretty neat when we come to define Canada. Look at our travel brochures. We show moccasins and Indian handicrafts. However, when it comes down to things like the Constitution, whether there will be low-level flights which disrupt the Inuit in northern Quebec or Labrador, or whether we will protect trapping, hunting and sealing areas, then we are not so cute. Then we say that is just tradition, not a real economy.
There is a real aboriginal economy that has never been recognized. That fact reflects the kind of disregard and lack of respect we have shown for aboriginal people. We are missing a tremendous resource of scientific knowledge on the part of aboriginal people, whether it be the Inuit in the high Arctic or Indian peoples across Canada. They have a knowledge of the land, of our renewable resources, of patterns of climate and environment which we disregard because somehow it is not seen as scientific. Again it is because we choose to look only at aboriginal people from our cultural bias. We have decided what is right and we will tell them what is right.
Arctic sovereignty is in the news a lot. What we need to do is get more submarines up there! Maybe we should have military bases. More troops. Sure, we will put a military base in Nanisivik and to the Inuit we say: You can be the janitors. That is not good enough. We have had a presence in the North for thousands of years. We have a legitimacy in the North through the occupation of the Inuit and aboriginal peoples.
Then we have native economic development programs. We have a four-year program involving S345 million, but just as it is nearly over, they can spend only 40 per cent of the funds. Yet look at the statistics on unemployment and training.
I would like to close with one other very important issue, that of justice and things like the Marshall case and the killing of J. J. Harper in Manitoba. Many of us have known for years the statistics concerning the over-representation of aboriginal populations in our jails. This really means we must address national problems with national solutions. In both economic development and justice we must have a national focus and an inquiry into these issues and why they remain.
Finally, many statistics have been given here today about high unemployment, mortality rates and so on. I will not repeat them but I will say there is a strength in the aboriginal community from which we can learn and which we have rejected by our cultural blindness through our rejection of Canada's first culture. We can do much better, and I strongly support this motion and say to the people of Canada and this House that with the political will we can have justice for aboriginal people on aboriginal terms that will work for aboriginal people.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for her comments on the life of the aboriginal people, particularly as

she knows them in the Yukon. As she pointed out, it is a national question.
She made reference to several things that I would be interested in having her explain a little more fully. She referred to land claims and the policies and procedures worked out for handling them. I think she suggested they were too narrow and that she would like to see them widened.
She also referred to the transfer programs that were part of the move toward so-called self-government and the rules imposed upon the Indian bands. She implied that some of those rules may have been inappropriate.
I would like her to explain further about the land claims guidelines and the rules for the transfer programs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTED DAY, S. O. 82-RIGHTS OF ABORIGINAL PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question from my colleague because it is a very complex matter. The question of land claims and transfer of programs relates to the whole question of self-government and control over one's life.
First, the narrow mandate of land claims. Certainly there are basic issues in land claims such as self-government, land quantum, and cash compensation in certain instances. Of course, it is a negotiating process, and I am not suggesting that it should not be, that the aboriginal people tell you what they want and you say that is fine. It is a negotiating process. However, why in 15 years, in the case of the Yukon and many other land claims across Canada, has there not been a resolution of the problem? We have for good or ill, most of us think for ill, a trade agreement with the U.S. That did not go on for 15 years. When there was a will to get a trade agreement, we got a trade agreement. We can do the same thing in land claims. It simply means widening the mandate to some degree to allow the negotiators to negotiate on specific items and simply give them more latitude.
These negotiations require the giving up of some power. Ottawa cannot continue to control Indian peoples. Everyone at every level is simply going to have to realize that. We will be a healthier and stronger country when aboriginal people have control over that.
With respect to the programs, I will just give an example because I referred to it in my speech to some extent. An example is the National Native Alcohol and Drug Abuse Program. This is an extremely important program with a number of teaching, treatment, and counselling programs. In my area, and indeed nationally, native people have been negotiating with the federal Government to have control of this program. However, the Department of National Health and Welfare continues to run the program. It pulls the strings and says: "You will do it our way".
Well, "our way", and in that I include myself and my culture, has not worked. It concerns me that we continue to repeat the mistakes of history, whether in the transfer of child welfare services to aboriginal people or the transfer of other

programs. We insist that doing it our way works. We have heard numerous statistics today that indicate that doing it our way does not work. We must begin to take a more realistic view and accept that there is a cultural dimension.

subsubtopic: ALLOTED DAY, S. O. 82-RIGHTS OF ABORIGINAL PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on the motion before the House and perhaps highlight one of the issues raised in this debate, the problems associated with it, and why it is mentioned by the mover of the motion. If outlining the problem does not get too boring, I would like to give a solution to the people who read Hansard and are involved with the federal programs which are referred to in this motion.
First, this is a very fine motion. It involves not only aboriginal people of Canada but all people in Canada. When you point out that the Government has not done enough for the provision of adequate shelter, health and educational facilities, basic water and sewage treatment facilities, adequate employment and training opportunities, and the financial resources to develop fully economic and human resources, that would cover more than half of Canada. It would certainly cover the rural and poorer areas of a country.
I do not want to get into generalizations. I am not very good at the generalizations and philosophical arguments which some may put forward on this motion. I do not have time for philosophical arguments because there is so much to be done with regard to specifics. There are so many requests which come into an MP's office on specific problems.
I want to refer to subsection (c) which refers to basic water and sewage treatment facilities. Only today I read a letter from Chief Calvin Francis, the Chief of the northern part of Gander Bay, Newfoundland, in my riding. He was complaining about this particular aspect of life in his area. This rings true for a great many areas of Newfoundland and other parts of Canada.
The complexity of the problem depends upon which province you are in. In other words, there are provincial laws and federal laws, but the provincial laws differ in practically every province with regard to what you must do to try to solve the problem. I will deal only with the provision of basic water and sewage treatment facilities.
We are talking about Canada in 1988. In Canada today we have thousands of children who drink contaminated water. Whose responsibility is it to try to correct this problem? Whose responsibility is it to make such communities conform with Ottawa where you are able to drink water from a tap or flush a toilet? A great many areas of Canada do not have such privileges and it leads to an incredible number of problems.
The area of Gander Bay to which I referred a moment ago is similar to a great many other areas referred to by this motion. There are many problems involved with this. One is that you are confronted with various provincial guidelines. For example, you must have an engineering study done before you can tackle a water and sewage problem. Number one, who is going to pay
for the engineering study? Number two, the engineering study must be passed by the provincial Department of the Environment. Number three, the Department of Health must inspect the water source. Number four, if in examining the engineering study the Department of the Environment and the Department of Health determines that you must have sewage treatment facilities along the water system which is to be installed, you have one big problem because for 15 or 20 homes in a rural area sewage treatment facilities cost perhaps a quarter of a million dollars, and that is a fairly cheap sewage system. The question arises as to who is going to pay for that.
Normally a town or city, through taxes, pays off a loan obtained through a municipal financing system of the provincial government or directly through a bank. That cannot happen in the areas about which we are speaking because there is either a band council, such as in the case of Mr. Calvin Francis, or you must become incorporated in one way or another.
You may be lucky enough to get a grant to pay for the engineering study. There is only one place which I know of that you can get the grant, and that is through some provincial agency. When you do that there is a condition on the grant. If you get a grant from a provincial financing agency in some provinces, you must sign a piece of paper saying that once the system is completed you will impose property taxes. That is the law in most provinces in Canada. If you receive taxpayers' money in the form of grants you must impose property taxes on the homes which will be served by that water and sewage system.
That applies to most provinces of Canada in which you must have an engineering study in order to undertake any sort of water works. In other words, you cannot simply connect 40 or 50 houses to a water system for which you have found the money from a source such as a federal works program. It cannot be done.
A group of people in a small rural area say that they would like to be able to turn on a water tap in their houses in the same way as people in the cities and large towns do. They say: "We want bathrooms in our houses just like those in the towns and cities". The first thing to do is apply for some money because it cannot be done without money. It cannot be done only with volunteers because money is needed to buy pipe, dynamite, other materials to put in the lines.
One used to be able to apply for a normal grant program of the federal or provincial government. There used to be a works program through which people would be put to work to start the water system. I am talking about these programs as they relate to people who live in communities with no water or sewage system as we know it, but a well for a group of two or three houses and septic tanks behind the houses.
A community like that which seeks to install a water system can apply for what is called the job development program of
March 17, 1988

the federal Government. It is the largest works program of the federal Government, and involves millions of dollars. Advertisements state that communities wishing to make improvements should apply under that program.
The only problem is that the Government has converted it into a training program so that those hired under the program must be trained for a certain skill. How do you train someone to dig a ditch? I believe a person could be trained in one day to dig a ditch and install a water line. Therefore, the federal Government does not fund water and sewer system projects as they used to be funded years ago. It will no longer fund water and sewer systems to completion under its largest direct funding grant program because it stipulates that employees must have classroom experience every day on the job, which simply cannot be done in this case. Let us keep in mind that these communities consist of relatively poor people. Any rural doctor will say that today, children in many of these rural communities have to drink contaminated water every morning.
What is the second largest program under which these communities can apply for grants without having to pay them back? It is a program called Section 38, which provides grants to community groups to help toward useful community improvements. The material costs under that program are higher than the job development program and also have certain restrictions.
In order to get money to put in the water and sewer system under Section 38, only those drawing unemployment insurance can be hired. Some MPs just might be foolish enough to promote this program. The fact is that workers who have been hired under that program of the federal Government must be laid off when their unemployment insurance benefits have run out. The MP will have to explain that the reason his constituent did not get unemployment insurance benefits from all the work he did on this summer project is that it was uninsurable employment. As a result, the MP has intentionally put that man on welfare, since that is his only alternative.
I know of only one direct funding program that is fairly universal in Canada. It is a provincial program that is paid fifty-fifty through a recovery system with the federal Government. It is referred to by various names by provinces across Canada. It is usually called the community development program, but I have seen it referred to as the community action program in Ontario and other places. In my opinion and in the opinion of those who work under these programs, it should be called the welfare program.
We have already determined that we cannot do the project through the job development program because we are not allowed to train people to dig a ditch. We have the second largest program, Section 38, to install the water and sewer system, but those we hire will end up on welfare after receiving uninsurable employment.
Unfortunately, the welfare program is designed simply to take people off welfare and put them on unemployment
Supply
insurance. In other words, when they qualify for unemployment insurance they lose their jobs under the welfare program, and there is no material cost. Talk about intentionally putting people on unemployment insurance.
Most of the communities covered under this motion deal with people who are what we call "repeaters" of unemployment insurance. If a private employer went out and took someone on social assistance, gave them exactly 10 weeks or 20 weeks, just enough to qualify for unemployment insurance, that employer would be brought into court and charged. It is against the law. Provincial Governments do it all the time. In every single provincial budget that I have ever seen there is always enough money to take 10,000 or 20,000 people off social assistance and put them on unemployment insurance. The grants run just long enough for someone to qualify for unemployment insurance and then they are laid off.
Here we have the only three grant programs, not loans, available to communities in Canada covered by this motion to put in a water and sewer system, for people drinking contaminated water, and the three programs are not useable for putting in those vital services. That is the bottom line with all these organizations since this Government took over. Previously we were able to do that under the largest program, the Canada Works Program.
The bottom line is that this motion deplores the Government for its failure to address the needs of the aboriginal people of Canada, including the provision of adequate shelter, health care, educational facilities, basic water and sewage treatment facilities and so on and so on. There is no way now they can get money through normal government programs to put in water and sewer systems. There is no possible way. However, if they wished to do something else in the community, they can do it. If they can take someone into a classroom and teach him or her a lesson every day before they go out on the job, they can get some money.
In conclusion, let me say, without going into detail, that the other programs operate in approximately the same way. We have rural and native housing programs. I could write a book on rural and native housing problems. We know inside out and upside down every regulation that has been changed over the years. The new program is called the RRAP program. It is not very well known in Ottawa, Toronto or Montreal, but mention it in any of the rural areas and everyone knows what you are talking about. Yet that program has been so restricted under this Government that it is practically non-existent.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the previous speaker for pointing out so adequately the bind so many aboriginal communities are in. I think he has delineated one program, the water and sewer program, and, as he said at the conclusion, it certainly affects many other programs. The obstacles that are set up are worthy of an Olympic hurdle race for the people who try to take advantage of them. Usually, if

March 17, 1988
Supply
they could take advantage of any of the programs about which the Hon. Member spoke, they would never be completed because the program would end and they would have half a sewer and half a water system.
The speaker mentioned housing. Certainly those of us who have been involved with the issue of housing for aboriginal communities, especially the joint housing projects between CMHC and DIA, have found it an extremely frustrating process. The intent of the program may have been good initially but it is causing many problems in aboriginal communities. Under the guaranteed loans through CMHC, many of the aboriginal people are paying very exorbitant rents. In my own riding we recently had something like a 25 per cent increase in rents in one year under those jointly funded programs.
Would the Member tell us what his experience has been with the joint housing program of DIA and CMHC? How would he comment on that particular program and its success in dealing with the housing needs of aboriginal people?

The one thing that is really frustrating to the person who is in the House-and there are all kinds of problems in actually getting into the property in the beginning-is the amount of rent one has to pay is constantly under revision. It is constantly changing. The real problem, I believe, with all of the funding programs that are in existence for native peoples and non-native peoples, is that there are provincial inputs and federal inputs and there are local inputs. What one would have to do is remove the interference from outside and allow local authorities to change the regulations. A person who made $20,000 last year, living in a subsidized rental unit, but today is on unemployment insurance, is watching the rent double from last year. That is absolutely atrocious. The objections that were placed by Chief Calvin Francis today in his communications to me is that they only qualify for housing under the rural and native programs and the cut-down version of the RRAP program.
There are various elements in the RRAP program. One element is native, another element is handicapped and another is just your normal RRAP program. I still cannot figure it out. If one has a house, they will come in and fix up that house, but they will fix it up in such a way that the inspector says it must do for 15 years. In other words, even if you do not want it, you will get the side replaced or the chimney redone or the roof done. By the time it is all added up, under the new regulations brought in by the Conservative Government two years ago, you are left with receiving $5,000 free at the beginning but then having a mortgage of $10,000 which you could not possibly pay back. I must say I have cases before me, as I am sure do all Members of Parliament, where we have written to the Ministers responsible and asked for Ministerial intervention to get around certain regulations in the Act. I am hoping that the two Ministers in this House, to whom we have written regarding special cases under which the Minister has some
discretion, will intervene in those particular cases. I am hoping they will intervene.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development); Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: ALLOTED DAY, S. O. 82-RIGHTS OF ABORIGINAL PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to respond to the motion of the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy). When I look at the motion, I see that he obviously wants to lay on the back of this Government the plight of native people across Canada. When one has listened to what has been said in the House regarding the situation of native people in Canada, one cannot but find it outrageous that some people would try to blame this Government for a situation that has developed over a long time. I do not know why they do this. Perhaps it is to get rid of their own sense of culpability.
I listened to the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) making his statements. He was outrageous. If I were a native listening to this debate, I would be insulted. I would be insulted because what has been set out here today regarding our native people is not a reflection of the reality. That is not what is happening to our native people. This condemnation of the Government that the socialists have brought forward does not take into account the real situation and what the Government has been doing.
I was listening to the alleged cuts in spending being outlined by Members opposite. Canadians must know what we are talking about here. When we talk about registered Indians under the Indian Act we are talking, in 1986, about 387,000 people living on and off reserves. We are talking about our Inuit population, which is about 30,000 people scattered over all of northern Quebec, Canada and the territories. That is what we are talking about.
When we talk about money and alleged cuts, it just does not hold. I do not know if Hon. Members opposite and I are looking at the same public account books or not. In the books that I have looked at, I saw that in 1983-84 aboriginal expenditures in Canada were $2,461,000,000. At that time that was 2.77 per cent of total government expenditures. Today, in 1987-88 aboriginal expenditures are $3,863,000,000, which is 4 per cent of total government expenditures.

One does not have to be a genius to understand that this is not a reduction, but an increase in expenditures.
Mr. Speaker, Hon. Members of the House are well aware of the importance of economic development. Today, my Government colleagues, especially the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), have mentioned the efforts made by the Government to improve the situation of our native people through various programs.
I take this opportunity to point out that Hon. Members from both sides of the House are well aware of the importance of
March 17, 1988

economic development in the case of aboriginal Canadians. Aboriginal people want to have more control over their daily activities, the type of control which other Canadians take for granted. That is why their economic development and selfgovernment are really a priority for our Government, something the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) emphasized on several occasions.
Mr. Speaker, our Government believes that entrepreneurship must be the motor of long term economic growth and job creation. Our small businesses account for 80 per cent of all jobs created in Canada and within our Indian communities. Our best hope remains in the ambition and creativity demonstrated by Indian entrepreneurs. And this Government launched major initiatives in that area.
Mr. Speaker, the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs and the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion have such programs. We offer concrete and tangible support to native entrepreneurs, in the form of training and financial assistance to help them establish new businesses and expand existing ones.
For instance, during this fiscal year alone, expenditures in the area of economic development of native businesses and economic institutions will be in the order of $150 million. According to our files, there are in Canada more than 4,000 businesses owned and operated by Indians. Most of them are reserve-based, and their numbers are increasing rapidly. For instance, during fiscal 1986 alone, we supported the start-up in Canada of more than 300 new Indian businesses. Most of them relied on upfront financial assistance from the Canadian Government, either to supply the capital needed or finance their loans, either directly or through the Indian Economic Development Fund, or again through departmental loan guarantees.
Hon. Members will know that the Indian Economic Development Fund is an important source of support for new businesses. It provides both training and advisory and support services to Indian entrepreneurs. The Fund was established in 1970 to support the development of viable Indian economic initiatives. Last year, the Fund helped some 900 Indian businesses get established and win a place in the market. Moreover, the $200 million invested over the last three years by the Native Economic Development Program and the special agreements on rural and farming development, and the subsidiary agreements on northern development, administered by the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, have had a significant impact on the development and maintenance of a native private sector in native communities across Canada.
I would like to emphasize more specifically that the Government made significant progress in allowing natives to take control of their own economic development. We have provided more than $100 million of funds to Indian financial institutions from across the country. Those financial institutions will play an important role in the future to finance the growth of Indian businesses through loans or equity financing.
Supply
Apart from the support provided to native business development corporations by the Indian Affairs Department, we help Native people to establish a system of consulting and financial services, managed by native people, independant and able to answer the needs and hopes of Indians.

Indian Affairs and Northern Development provides ongoing advice and financial assistance to Indian bands for the management of their natural resources. Resource development, forestry, fishing, agriculture and wildlife represent significant potential sources of income and employment for Indians. In forestry, for example, changes being developed to timber regulations and future increased federal investment in Indian forestry management will put Indian forestry back on a solid footing after decades of neglect, notwithstanding what the previous Member who spoke before me was talking about. The Government's strong relationship with the provinces has resulted in Indian management of provincial forest land adjacent to reserves.
Oil and gas is another important base for economic selfreliance in western Canada. Indian bands and government officials are currently reviewing together the existing management and regulatory regime relating to oil and gas. We are confident that ways will be found to improve the benefits accruing to Indians from their own oil and gas resource development.
In the meantime, an oil and gas branch has been formed within the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The human resources dedicated to this activity alone have been expanded sixfold. Top-notch professionals are being recruited to ensure the best possible return now and over the long term to Indians.
Many Indian reserves have good potential for mineral development. These have been hampered by legal and structural barriers inherent in the Indian Act, but also by a lack of access to private sector capital and by disputes with some provinces regarding control over royalties and other financial benefits. These are being addressed for the first time and progress is being made.

As a matter of fact, the federal Government, in co-operation with native people and their economic organizations, is helping isolated native communities to benefit from economic development opportunities. For example, we support the creation of service industries in those communities due to the implementation of construction and infrastructure projects. These projects helped create 3,700 jobs for Indians. We also encourage local hiring in order to maximize the opportunities created at the local level through vesting of existing federal programs.
Mr. Speaker, we have in Canada a wrong idea about native businesses. I was extremely disappointed to hear NDP and Liberal Members speak in today's debate of natives as if all their endeavors always ended in failure, as if they were

March 17, 1988
Supply
incapable of doing something right and as if they had never made any progress.
Contrary to what the NDP and the Liberals would have Canadians believe, many native businesses are successful. Native entrepreneurs are talented and ambitious and their success rate is high. For example, Econobois, a construction material retailer in the Huron village of Quebec, employs 25 people and has annual sales of more than $5.5 million.
Micmac Industries of Big Gove, in my home Province of New Brunswick, employs 14 persons and has sales of $1.6 million; Lasso Contracting Ltd. of Fort McMurray, Alberta, employs 15 people and has sales of $3 million; the Co-op Store in Fort Hope, Ontario, which is owned and managed by Indians, employs six people and has sales of $2 million; Antsanen Enterprises has sales of close to $800,000 and provides eight jobs in the small Northlands Band in northern Manitoba. I could go on and list successful native businesses in this country. That list will become much longer as we remove the legal and structural impediments to native economic development, as we help more native people to develop good management and occupational skills, as we work to increase funding from private sector sources, and as we improve education levels.
In speaking of removing impediments and barriers to economic development, for a few moments I wish to dwell on how the Government has responded to a call by 115 band councils to amend the Indian Act. Following a two year process of full consultation with Indian communities across Canada, on March 9, 1988, the Government introduced legislation to give bands taxing powers on conditionally surrendered reserve lands. The Bill would also make it possible for Indians to mortgage long term leases on designated reserve bands. This is important legislation, and it is Indian-led legislation. The credit goes to Chief Clarence Jules of the Kamloops Band who started the process, and who has dedicated himself to seeing it through. This Bill has widespread support. Yesterday at a meeting in Toronto the Confederacy of First Nations debated the Bill and passed a resolution in its support.
Not every band will want or need to take advantage of those changes, but for those that do, it will permit them to economically develop parts of their reserves for commercial, industrial, residential, or recreational purposes. Indians should be much better able to obtain loans and to recover their investment in infrastructure or services. They will also be able to govern developed land as an integral part of their reserve. This will expand the economic base of the reserve and the business and employment opportunities for band members.
It is practical changes like those that are as important as the direct financial investments that I spoke of earlier. I trust that Members on all sides of the House will facilitate the passage of
this Indian inspired legislation in order that bands like the Kamloops Band can get on with their business.
The Government is criticized for not paying attention to the problem of unemployment among native people, particularly those who live on reserves. The facts tell a different story. All day we have heard the socialists and the Liberals tell us it is only a question of money. If it is only a question of money, surely when the Grits were in the process of bankrupting the country they would have solved the problems. It is not only a question of money.
Since 1985, the Government's expenditures on native adult training and labour force adjustment assistance have exceeded $600 million. The Canadian Jobs Strategy of the Canadian Employment and Immigration Commission, the Indian community human resources strategy, and education programs of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development are the main vehicles for helping individuals develop their skills, find jobs, and for assisting Indian leaders to establish and implement plans and strategies to address training and employment problems in their communities.
The Indian community human resources strategy alone has provided full-time academic upgrading and vocational training to 6,000 Indians since 1985. This is a key activity given the strong, proven relationship between academic attainment and employment. Training on the job and entrepreneurial development have been particularly effective. There have been 3,300 unemployed Indians who have benefited from training on the job, and presently most have ongoing jobs. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development's 1987 youth entrepreneurship training has graduated 169 persons, 71 of whom are already in business or shortly will be.
As native people achieve higher levels of education, they will be presented with more opportunities for private sector employment. Education has influenced the number and types of businesses established and operated by aboriginal people. Almost 80,000 Indian students are enrolled in elementary, secondary, and post-secondary education programs in Canada today. Each year, approximately 750 Indian people graduate from colleges and universities. Why do I quote that figure? Almost 11 years ago, in 1977, federal funding for Indian postsecondary education was less than $8 million. This year it is expected to reach $93.5 million. That is another clear reflection of the Government's commitment to Indian education.
Indian management skills have been recognized as national skill shortages within the Canadian Jobs Strategy, thus permitting more training in that area. This will not only help business managers, but also community and tribal Indian administrators of devolved government programs.
Government training and employment programs are progressively being devolved to local community control. This is the case with the Indian community human resources program, and increasingly so with respect to the Canadian Jobs Strategy. In the coming year we expect to make further advances with the introduction of initiatives focused on moving
March 17, 1988

Indian social assistance recipients into full-time employment, and providing more support to seasonal labour activities on reserves for housing, construction, and the like.
When we reflect on today's debate and on the question of native people, no one has pointed out the fact that unlike the previous Government, when this Government took office it listened to native people across Canada. As a priority we adopted the pursuance of self-government. As the previous Government tried to do, we have not attempted to impose anything upon our native people, upon Indians. They will develop at their own pace. They do not want any Government to come in and impose anything on them.
In terms of economic and social development we recognize as a Government that more work must be done. We must strive to do even better. Elowever, I think we are on the right course. Very little credit goes to our native people if we try to make political hay of their plight. Therefore I encourage all Hon. Members of the House to vote against this NDP motion.

On one hand I agree with him when he says that the problems and issues which the Government is trying to address did not begin in 1984. They are of a very long standing history. The previous Liberal Government has no better record in that regard.
I should like to address a little more fully the issue of training and post-secondary education in general. It is an area in which I have been involved over the years. I think I know first-hand some of the problems and successes in this area. I know that there have been on the job training programs, but I would be very interested in knowing, if the Minister has the figure, how many of the 3,300 people trained on the job actually now have full-time employment.
I would also like to remind the Minister that many training and educational programs have not addressed the fundamental problems which exist. He mentioned the Canadian Jobs Strategy which is now cutting back significantly, as the Minister well knows, so that the upgrading needed by not only native Canadians but others is not available. Funds are being cut back from the community colleges which often offered those courses and they are being transferred to private industry. Literacy programs, again not just for aboriginal Canadians but for many others, receive very little funding. I think most of us who have had any experience with the educational system would agree that it has certainly failed aboriginal people.
There is a necessity for training and upgrading programs which unfortunately are expensive and almost provide a parallel system of education in one sense, because there is so much to be done in the area. I agree that some things have been done. We have had programs like the Saskatchewan Indian Federated College, the Blue Quills College in Alberta, and the Native Cultural Centre in British Columbia. There
Supply
have been some good educational programs, but the fact remains that about 20 per cent of the Indian children growing up today will complete secondary school, whereas about 75 per cent of the general Canadian population will complete secondary school.
Ihave two questions for the Minister surrounding the real success in full-time employment of on the job training, which again is often short term, and the funding of post-secondary programs that are often uncertain and go from year to year rather than on a permanent basis.
