speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-ACQUIRED RIGHTS OF SASKATCHEWAN FRANCOPHONES-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE IN TRANSLATING LAWS-TRANSLATION OF SASKATCHEWAN STATUTES- REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 25 last the Supreme Court of Canada came out with a historic ruling which might completely alter the Canadian political scenery.
As you may recall, I directed a question to the Government to know its reaction to this decision which I would qualify as being very important to us Canadians.
The Supreme Court ruled that the Province of Saskatchewan has been bilingual since 1905 with respect to its legislative assembly and its courts, which means that any elected Member in that province has the right to speak French or English in the legislative assembly and that all provincial legislation must be passed in both French and English to be valid.
The court also ruled that an individual is entitled to be tried in his or her own language before the courts of the Province of Saskatchewan. Understandably, Mr. Speaker, the decision makes quite a change to the political scene because apparently, in addition to Saskatchewan, the neighbouring Province of Alberta would be subject to the same ruling because it came into being pursuant to identical legislation.
Francophones see this as a major step towards full recognition of their rights which have been trampled on for 85 years. Francophone communities out west have been fighting for decades just to survive in French. The Supreme Court has just confirmed their rights and given them some hope. I say some hope because the court ruling acknowledges the fact that both provinces can legally pass a bilingual law whose effect would be to exempt them from complying with section 110 (Northwest Territories) and thus to deprive francophone minorities of their rights.
This greatly complicates the political scene when we realize that these two provinces have never been too generously disposed toward Francophones. They went along only after quite a lot of arm twisting.
That is why before the Supreme Court came down with its decision the recognition of these basic rights had required many long years of struggle before the courts. These legal battles are not only long, but expensive and exhausting, for they drain a lot of energy. In the case of Father Mercure who went to the Supreme Court of Canada, it took him five years from 1983 to 1988 before obtaining justice. It required a lot of dedication, because at every stage of the legal process, Francophones were told that they had no rights as Francophones in Saskatchewan.
Mr. Speaker, they never gave up. They kept on fighting and appealing to higher courts; they took other steps and incurred other expenses. Faced with constant obstacles, others might have given up. I think that we should congratulate them for showing such determination in getting their basic rights recognized.
Now that they have won, they should not let the legislatures abdicate their responsibilities and deprive them of that right the Supreme Court has recognized. The Federal Government should show political leadership and offer these two provinces assistance to deal with this situation.
March 17, 1988

It would be totally useless to force them to translate all the legislation adopted since 1905, because it would not serve the public interest or the common good. It would be a waste of public funds, because there is probably a lot of obsolete statutes which do not need to be translated.
Of course, if the provinces choose to take the easy road, they will introduce and pass a legislation stating that the province is unilingual and strictly English-speaking, that is they would repeal section 110. In doing so, the francophones would loose their rights without any recourse. It would be legal, though very unfair, not to say cynical, on the part of both provinces which, it will be remembered, passed the constitutional resolution proceeding from the Meech Lake agreement.
By endorsing the Meech Lake agreement, both provinces firmly undertook before the rest of Canada to protect the linguistic rights of their minorities which is as you know a basic characteristic of our country.
They would be ill-advised to pass a legislation withdrawing the almost century-old rights of their francophones. It would probably be legal but it would not be fair.
We have to hurry, Mr. Speaker, because we know that Alberta is about to introduce legislation. Indeed, a dispatch from the Canadian Press confirmed on March 16 that the Government House Leader intends to table such a Bill. We are still waiting for the details of that legislation. But the worst is to be feared, Mr. Speaker, when one knows that in June last, that same legislature in Alberta passed a resolution to limit the use of French in its proceedings-the Piquette case-to such a point that permission is required to use one of the official languages of this country.
The solution would be to retain section 110, even to enshrine it in our Constitution, so that Francophones would feel protected and well treated in those provinces in the future. In exchange for an agreement on partial translation of the major provincial statutes, and not all of them, those two provinces should undertake to increase their services in French to their residents. We would thus save considerable amounts of time and money while making better use of federal grants to be allocated not only to protect, Mr. Speaker, but to promote the French culture in Saskatchewan and Alberta.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-ACQUIRED RIGHTS OF SASKATCHEWAN FRANCOPHONES-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE IN TRANSLATING LAWS-TRANSLATION OF SASKATCHEWAN STATUTES- REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will recall the fundamental decision handed down by the Supreme Court of Canada in Mercure vs. the Attorney General of Saskatchewan. The Supreme Court ruled that Section 110 of the Northwest Territories Act of 1891 was still valid in the Province of Saskatchewan. In doing so, the Court pointed out that the statutes of the Province were invalid but the principle of the rule of law would keep the existing laws temporarily in effect. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, the Court stated that the language requirements could be modified. It was up to the Province to pass legislation to change the present legal
Adjournment Debate
situation as defined by the Court. Only the Province could determine which option it preferred.
We recognize and respect the Province's autonomy in this respect, and we are very much aware of the divergent interests involved in this decision. In fact, these interests deserve special attention, and we realize that the Province cannot reach a decision without proper reflection.
At the same time, the Government of Canada fully approves the equality of status and use of English and French across Canada. In this respect, the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) initiated certain measures last fall, well before the Mercure case, and some positive consultation has taken place. Since the Supreme Court's decision, there has been further discussion about integrating the implementation of the decision with the broader issues.
The implementation of the Court's decision is expected to require substantial amounts of human, technical and financial resources. Mr. Speaker, we wish to repeat here in the House that the Government of Canada is prepared to help the Province accomplish this task, using the means at its disposal. We are consulting closely with the Government of Saskatchewan to determine in what way we can be most useful, if the Province should request our assistance.
Mr. Speaker, in the days following the decision in the Mercure case, the Government of Canada reiterated to Canadians its position, announced when Bill C-72 was tabled, that it maintained its policy of co-operating with the provinces and the Territories to ensure that the most important provincial, territorial and municipal services would be available in English and in French. We still believe that one of the most urgent priorities for minority language communities across this country is full implementation of minority language educational rights as enshrined in Section 23 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. This is the most important need of the Francophone community, including that of Saskatchewan, and indeed an area where we can be most useful. While we recognize the Province's jurisdiction over education and provincial services, we shall indeed continue to consult and cooperate with the provincial authorities for the very purpose reflected in Section 16 of the Charter, namely to promote the equality of status and use of French and English.

CANADA HEALTH ACT-EQUAL ACCESS- MINISTER'S POSITION/ADMINISTRATION OF ACT

subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-ACQUIRED RIGHTS OF SASKATCHEWAN FRANCOPHONES-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE IN TRANSLATING LAWS-TRANSLATION OF SASKATCHEWAN STATUTES- REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gave me great concern that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), in his reply to my question on March 8, did not seem to address the crux of the problem. Certainly I have great concern about what is happening, not just to the women of this country but to our health care system in general. In the 1986-87 Canada Health Act annual report, the Minister said that his department has been following carefully recent developments in provincial programs. Examples of these included the removal of insured coverage for some health

March 17, 1988
Adjournment Debate
services and charges to patients for services which may not necessarily be medically required. A number of issues related to possible non-compliance were identified and subsequently resolved, while some cases are currently under review.
We now know that the attempt to restrict certain services in the Province of British Columbia has not been allowed by the court. Therefore it seems to me that if we are going to have an effective Canada Health Act, the Minister must act on that ruling.
We are greatly concerned that the principles of the Canada Health Act are not being upheld. The principles of public administration, comprehensiveness, universality, portability and accessibility are the ones at which we are looking.
With regard to accessibility, it says insured health services on uniform terms and conditions and reasonable access by insured persons to insured health services unprecluded or unimpeded, either directly or indirectly, by charge or other means. Surely it is quite clear, after the Supreme Court decision, that there should be access to these services for women right across the country.
It seems to me that the Government is reluctant to implement the Canada Health Act. New Democrats have never said that abortion on demand should be the policy in place. We have said, though, that it should be equally accessible to women across the country and that we should not be discriminated against on the basis of geography or whether we are rich or poor. That is the issue on which we are trying to get an answer from the Minister. The Minister should take that responsibility as the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp). He is responsible for ensuring that the Canada Health Act is implemented.
The practice of de-insuring important health care services must be stopped. We have seen this happen in Alberta and know that it can be the beginning of the erosion of the whole medical health system in Canada. With something as clear as the Supreme Court decision it is very important that the Minister of National Health and Welfare exercise his responsibility to ensure that there is accessibility across the country.
If we conclude that debate, we can go on to the issue of services for women which would provide some prevention. We could talk about counselling and contraceptive information. I am concerned that the Minister is not fulfilling his responsibility of discovering where there is not accessibility. If this responsibility is fulfilled Canadian women can get the services which they need.
Under the Canada Health Act we could have pre-abortion and post-abortion counselling and contraceptive information. These things would be useful in reducing the number of abortions. However, that will not happen as long as the Minister is playing around with the fundamental principles of the Canada Health Act.
We have been getting answers like: "I do not want to give an opinion to the House now" and "We are going to have to look at it for a while". Surely with the Supreme Court decision which has been handed down the Minister has a responsibility. There have been two court decisions now and the time has come when we must look at the implications of non-accessibility and how they erode the Canada Health Act.
I ask that the Minister respond to us on this side of the House by telling us how he is going to implement the Canada Health Act in order that the principles which have been put in place, which are the true values of Canadian society, will be upheld.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-ACQUIRED RIGHTS OF SASKATCHEWAN FRANCOPHONES-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE IN TRANSLATING LAWS-TRANSLATION OF SASKATCHEWAN STATUTES- REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight is the night I reply to questions concerning the Supreme Court!
The minister of Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), a minister responsible for the Canada Health Act, is most aware that the provinces, as is their right under the Constitution, are developing their policies on the delivery of abortion services.
This in neither completely unusual nor expected, since Canada consists of twelve provinces and territories which have different needs in relation to their economic, social, cultural and geographical requirements.
We have a national health care system because of federal-provincial co-operation, commitment and willingness to ensure that Canadians have reasonable access to insured health services without financial or other barriers. The system is based on a respect for the powers, rights, privileges or authorities vested in Canada or the provinces.
This reality has very specific implications for the application of the Canada Health Act and the principles it embodies. The provinces are responsible for the provision of health care services, and it is not within the powers of the federal Government to dictate to provinces what those health services must be, or how they should be delivered.
However, the provinces do have an obligation to satisfy the principles of the Canada Health Act before receiving federal cash contributions for the provision of insured health services. When questions do arise under the Act, experience has shown that both levels of government are willing to address the issue in a cooperative manner that will produce a satisfactory solution.
The Supreme Court decision has made it necessary for provincial and territorial governments to enter a difficult period of readjustment of their policies and procedures on abortion.
Access to the services on an insured basis is one key question in the debate. For some, access means that the service should be available everywhere to everyone without conditions or restrictions of any kind. Others view access to mean that the
March 17, 1988

service should only be available for very limited and specific reasons.
The Canada Health Act requires there to be reasonable access to medically necessary health services if a province is to qualify for full federal cash contributions. The determination of reasonable access must take into consideration all aspects related to the provision and delivery of any insured health service by a province. This could include an examination and understanding of provincial health care delivery resources, facilities, personnel, as well as a recognition of factors, i.e. geography, that may set practical limits on what health services are provided where.
The federal Government is committed to upholding principles of the Canada Health Act, and ensuring that provinces respect the act's provisions for federal funding. Changing developments in the area of abortion services are being closely followed.
IMMIGRATION-IMMIGRATION APPEAL BOARD HEARINGS- FEDERAL COURT OF CANADA RULING/REQUEST THAT BILL C-55 BE AMENDED

subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-ACQUIRED RIGHTS OF SASKATCHEWAN FRANCOPHONES-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE IN TRANSLATING LAWS-TRANSLATION OF SASKATCHEWAN STATUTES- REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a week ago I asked a question of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) on a matter of urgency in the refugee determination system. I asked, as reported at page 13602 of Hansard, whether the Minister:
-will now undertake to bring into Parliament an amendment to Bill C-55 which will assure members of the Immigration Appeal Board that they will have the normal rights and protection of tenure, that is, that they will not be dismissed during their term of office except for cause?
The Minister was so uninterested in the problem or the facts of the situation that he did not even know which Bill I was talking about. His answer was:
Mr. Speaker, I won't bring in any amendment to Bill C-84-
The Bill that is causing the trouble is Bill C-55. It has caused the Immigration Appeal Board to totally stop hearing refugee redeterminations. It is slowly bringing the Refugee Status Advisory Committee to a halt for the same reason. The reason is described by Judge Reed in her judgment at the Federal Court at Winnipeg. As it is stated in this article:
Mr. Matas argued before the court that the Government was opposing Mr. Sethi's application for refugee status at the same time as it was about to Tire' all the existing board members and select some of them, but not all, to become members of the new board.
The judge wrote:
This, it is argued, creates a reasonable apprehension of bias, an apprehension that the existing board members will tend to lean in favour of the Government's position.
Adjournment Debate
That was caused by the Government's passage through this House of Bill C-55, particularly Clause 38(1) and (7) which states:
Subject to this section, the members of the former Board and the members
of the former Committee cease to hold office on the commencement day.
No person appointed to hold office as a member of the former Board or of
the former Committee has any right to claim or receive any compensation,
damages, indemnity ...
In other words, they have no right to continue. They have lost the tenure which is normally considered essential to enable a judge or a person doing judge-like work to give the independent decision the law expects him or her to give.
In other words, as the court found, the Immigration Appeal Board, and the same applies to the Refugee Status Advisory Committee, are no longer to be trusted to be independent and impartial no matter what their good intentions may be because of this law that the Minister drove through the House of Commons.
That has caused not only an injustice to the individuals concerned, the refugee claimants and members of the board, but it is also causing a worsening of a serious backlog and administrative problem, which is a nightmare already, because of that foolish law and the Minister's foolish answer to my request.
The fact is that if the Minister will stop and think, he can very simply today, or if he is not here today, tomorrow, end this problem very easily. He can do justice, that is to say, he can restore the understanding of normal tenure so these judgelike people will not be dismissed during their term of office unless they give some special cause. That is the normal practice. At the same time, he can set the Immigration Appeal Board and the Refugee Status Advisory Committee functioning again very simply, by making a public announcement that he will move to amend Bill C-55-not Bill C-84; that is another battle-in Clause 38 so as to restore the normal right of tenure.
I urge the Minister to get off his high horse and let this process, which has had so many difficulties, get moving again.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to expand upon the reply given by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) to the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) on March 10, 1988. The Member knows that there are several legal issues raised by the Federal Court decision. These issues warrant thorough study by legal experts and a careful consideration by the Government. Such study and consideration has been undertaken and the Government will render its decision in due course. Until then, it would not be appropriate to comment on the case to which the Hon. Member refers.
I would, nevertheless, want to offer some comments about Bill C-55 and Bill C-84, which are designed to revise and

March 17, 1988
Adjournment Debate
expedite the refugee determination system and to curve the flagrant abuse of our immigration controls. The Hon. Member knows that Canada's refugee determination system is strained to the breaking point.
We have a backlog of more than 40,000 claims pending. The backlog is growing by 2,500 claims or more every month. Thousands of recent claimants arrived with fraudulent documents or with no documents at all.
Bill C-55 and Bill C-84 are essential first steps in restoring integrity to the refugee determination system. The new refugee determination system will maintain the existing high standards of fairness in keeping with Canada's humanitarian tradition. It affords to refugees the protection guaranteed under the
Convention and provides for efficient resolution of claims so that genuine refugees can get on with their lives in Canada.
The Immigration Act needs to be amended immediately. Bill C-84 and Bill C-55 are important parts of the solution to our backlog. These Bills, which are in the other place, cannot be allowed to languish there. I urge all Hon. Members to request all members of that other Chamber to accept their responsibilities and send the Bills forward.
